95992.e: Eclogite forms from basalt or gabbro only under very high pressure at great depth. The fact that it lies at the surface today shows how deep oceanic crust sank and was then raised again.
95992.m: Eclogite shows that oceanic crust sank deep down.

95993.q: Which nappe system does the highest peak in Switzerland, the Dufourspitze, belong to?
95993.e: The Dufourspitze in the Monte Rosa Massif consists of gneisses of the Penninic Monte Rosa Nappe. These rocks were buried deep during the formation of the Alps and raised again.
95993.m: The highest Swiss peak is made of Penninic gneiss.

95994.q: In which canton is the Penninic zone exposed as a deeply eroded stack of gneiss nappes, the Lepontine Dome?
95994.e: In the Leventina and the Maggia Valley, erosion has cut so deep that you can see the lowest Penninic gneiss nappes. These were strongly heated and transformed.
95994.m: In Ticino you can look deep into the belly of the Penninic nappes.

95995.q: Where do the rocks of the Austroalpine zone come from?
a: from the edge of the Adriatic Plate
95995.e: The Austroalpine zone formed the northern edge of the Adriatic Plate. During mountain building it was carried far to the north.
95995.m: The Austroalpine zone is a piece of the Adriatic continental margin.

95996.q: Which peak is the only four-thousander in the Eastern Alps and consists of Austroalpine rock?
95996.e: Piz Bernina is about 4049 m high and is built of rocks of the Bernina Nappe. It is the highest mountain in the Grisons.
95996.m: Piz Bernina is the only four-thousander in the Eastern Alps.

95997.q: Where in Switzerland does the Penninic zone appear in a tectonic window beneath the Austroalpine zone?
95997.e: In the Engadine Window near Scuol, erosion has cut through the Austroalpine nappes. Beneath them, Penninic Bündner schists appear.
95997.m: The Engadine Window shows Penninic rock beneath an Austroalpine nappe.

95998.q: What is the largest tectonic window of the Eastern Alps in Austria, where Penninic rock appears beneath the Austroalpine zone, called?
95998.e: In the Tauern Window, with the Grossglockner and Grossvenediger, Penninic and deeper units are exposed beneath the Austroalpine zone. It is about 175 km long.
95998.m: The Tauern Window is the largest window in the Eastern Alps.

95999.q: Which Austroalpine crystalline nappe builds the mountain group of the same name between the Prättigau and the Lower Engadine?
95999.e: The Silvretta Nappe consists of old gneiss and amphibolite from the Adriatic basement. It belongs to the Upper Austroalpine.
95999.m: The Silvretta is a piece of Austroalpine basement.

96000.q: What is a nappe in Alpine geology?
a: A large slab of rock that was pushed far over other rocks
A layer of snow that stays all year round
A thin layer of humus on the rock
A layer of cloud above the peaks
96000.e: During the formation of the Alps, packages of rock were sheared off and stacked on top of each other over many kilometres. The Err and Bernina Nappes in the Upper Engadine are examples.
96000.m: The Alps consist of rock nappes pushed on top of each other.

96001.q: Which Austroalpine unit forms a broad belt of Triassic limestones north of the Central Alps in Austria and Bavaria?
96001.e: The Northern Limestone Alps are sheared-off sedimentary nappes of the Upper Austroalpine. They include, for example, the Wetterstein Mountains and the Karwendel.
96001.m: The Northern Limestone Alps are Austroalpine sedimentary nappes.

96002.q: Why is it often said that the summit of the Matterhorn is “African”?
a: Its rock comes from the Adriatic Plate, which belongs to the African plate system
It was first climbed by African mountaineers
Its rock came with desert dust from the Sahara
It is as hot as an African mountain
96002.e: The upper part of the Matterhorn consists of gneisses of the Dent Blanche Nappe. This is counted as part of the Adriatic Plate, which was pushed over European rock during the formation of the Alps.
96002.m: The summit of the Matterhorn comes from the Adriatic side.

96003.q: What is the Aar Massif mainly made of?
96003.e: The Aar Massif is a piece of Europe's old crystalline basement. It was raised during the formation of the Alps and is now at the surface, for example at the Grimsel and around Göschenen.
96003.m: The Aar Massif consists of old crystalline rock such as granite and gneiss.

96004.q: How old is the Central Aar Granite compared with the Alps?
a: It is much older than the Alps
It formed at the same time as the Alps
It is younger than the Alps
It formed in the last ice age
96004.e: The Aar Granite solidified about 300 million years ago deep in the Earth's crust, during a much older mountain-building phase. During the formation of the Alps it was only raised and deformed.
96004.m: The Aar Granite is much older than the Alps themselves.

96005.q: Which crystalline massif borders the Aar Massif to the south, separated by the Urseren Valley?
96005.e: Between the Aar and Gotthard Massifs lies a narrow zone of soft rocks that shaped the Urseren Valley. Both massifs belong to the European basement.
96005.m: South of the Aar Massif comes the Gotthard Massif.

96006.q: Which peak, the highest in the Bernese Alps, consists of rocks of the Aar Massif?
96006.e: At 4274 m, the Finsteraarhorn is the highest mountain in the Bernese Alps. It is built of crystalline rocks of the Aar Massif.
96006.m: The Finsteraarhorn is the highest peak made of Aar Massif rock.

96007.q: In which cavities did the large rock crystals grow in the Aar Massif, for example at the Planggenstock?
96007.e: As the rock was raised, fissures opened up in which hot solutions circulated. Quartz and other minerals crystallised from them; in 2005 a particularly large crystal group was found at the Planggenstock.
96007.m: Alpine fissures are the treasure chambers of crystal hunters.

96008.q: Which geological unit does the Gotthard Base Tunnel pass through first after the north portal near Erstfeld?
96008.e: The tunnel begins near Erstfeld in the gneiss and granite of the Aar Massif. Further south come the Tavetsch intermediate massif, the Gotthard Massif and the Penninic gneisses.
96008.m: In the north, the base tunnel starts in the Aar Massif.

96009.q: Which UNESCO World Heritage Site lies largely in the Aar Massif?
96009.e: The World Heritage Site around the Aletsch Glacier and the Jungfrau region covers large areas of gneiss and granite of the Aar Massif. In the north there are also Helvetic limestones.
96009.m: The Aletsch region is mostly Aar Massif.

96010.q: Which granite landscape at the Grimsel Pass shows rocks of the Aar Massif beautifully polished by glaciers?
96010.e: The ice age glaciers polished the hard Grimsel granite into smooth, rounded humps. These roches moutonnées shape the landscape around the Grimselsee.
96010.m: At the Grimsel, roches moutonnées show the power of glaciers on granite.

96011.q: In which cantons does the Swiss Tectonic Arena Sardona, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, lie?
a: Glarus, St Gallen and the Grisons
96011.e: The area around Piz Sardona lies where Glarus, St Gallen and the Grisons meet. It has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2008.
96011.m: The Tectonic Arena Sardona lies in Glarus, St Gallen and the Grisons.

96012.q: What is special about the Glarus Thrust?
a: Older rock lies on younger rock.
Younger rock lies on older rock.
96012.e: At the thrust, rock from the Permian, about 260 to 300 million years old, lies on top of flysch that is only about 35 to 50 million years old. Normally younger layers lie on top.
96012.m: At Sardona the old lies on top of the young.

96013.q: What is the reddish rock from the Permian that was pushed over the younger flysch at Sardona called?
96013.e: Verrucano is a reddish conglomerate and sandstone from the Permian. Its name comes from Monte Verruca near Pisa.
96013.m: The red Verrucano forms the upper side of the Glarus Thrust.

96014.q: What happens twice a year at the Martinsloch in the Tschingelhörner?
a: The sun shines through the hole onto the church of Elm.
A waterfall plunges through the hole into the valley.
The wind whistles a note through the hole.
The moon sets exactly in the hole.
96014.e: In March and in autumn the sun is positioned so that its rays fall through the hole in the rock and briefly hit the church of Elm. The hole lies close to the thrust line.
96014.m: Twice a year the sun shines through the Martinsloch onto Elm.

96015.q: Which Zurich geologist long defended the idea of a “Glarus double fold” before accepting the thrust?
96015.e: Albert Heim first explained the reversed order of the layers with two folds facing each other. Only around 1902 did he accept the interpretation as a large thrust.
96015.m: Albert Heim finally gave up the Glarus double fold in favour of the thrust.

96016.q: Why was the Glarus Thrust so important for geology?
a: It showed that mountains form through rock nappes pushed over long distances
It proved that the Alps were formed by volcanoes
It showed that rocks are never older than 1000 years
It proved that there was never a sea in the Alps
96016.e: At the thrust, old rock lies above younger rock. It followed that huge packages of rock had been pushed over long distances, a basic idea of the nappe theory of the Alps.
96016.m: The Glarus Thrust helped people understand the nappe structure of the Alps.

96017.q: Roughly how far north was the upper mass of rock pushed at the Glarus Thrust?
96017.e: The rocks above the thrust surface were transported about 40 km to the north. This shows how enormous the forces of mountain building were.
96017.m: The Glarus Thrust pushed rock about 40 kilometres.

96018.q: How can you recognise the Glarus Thrust in the landscape?
a: As a sharp line in the rock faces where rocks of different colours meet
Only in drill cores deep underground
Only at the bottom of Lake Walen
By hot springs along the line
96018.e: The reddish Verrucano lies above the darker flysch. The boundary can be seen as a clear line on the Tschingelhörner, for example.
96018.m: The Glarus Thrust is visible as a line in the rock faces.

96019.q: Who is the Tethys Ocean named after?
96019.e: In Greek mythology, Tethys was a Titaness and sea goddess. At the end of the 19th century a geologist gave her name to the ancient sea.
96019.m: The Tethys bears the name of a Greek sea goddess.

96020.q: Which geologist coined the name Tethys in 1893 for the ancient sea between Eurasia and Gondwana?
96020.e: From marine deposits in the Alps and the Himalayas, Eduard Suess recognised that a large ocean had once lain there. He named it Tethys.
96020.m: Eduard Suess gave the Tethys its name.

96021.q: How was the Tethys positioned in relation to the supercontinent Pangaea?
a: as a sea bay open to the east
as an inland lake in the centre
as an icy sea at the North Pole
as a narrow river in the west
96021.e: Pangaea was roughly shaped like a C, with its opening facing east. The sea in this bay was the Tethys.
96021.m: The Tethys filled the large bay in the east of Pangaea.

96022.q: Which mountain ranges formed when the Tethys closed?
a: The Andes and the Rocky Mountains
The Appalachians and the Great Dividing Range
96022.e: As Africa, India and other plates drifted north, the Tethys was squeezed together. The mountains from the Alps to the Himalayas formed from its deposits.
96022.m: The Alps and the Himalayas are mountains from the Tethys Ocean.

96023.q: Which plates collided to form the Alps after the Tethys had disappeared?
a: The African and the Eurasian Plates
The Pacific and the North American Plates
The Indian and the Australian Plates
The South American and the Antarctic Plates
96023.e: Africa, with the Adriatic Plate in front of it, moved north towards Europe. The ocean in between was swallowed up and the Alps were folded up.
96023.m: The Alps formed from the collision of Africa and Europe.

96024.q: Which siliceous deep-sea rock made of tiny plankton skeletons is evidence in the Alps of the former deep Tethys Ocean?
96024.e: Radiolarite consists of the silica shells of radiolarians and was deposited at great ocean depths. It is found together with ophiolites, for example in the Grisons.
96024.m: Radiolarite is fossilised deep-sea mud of the Tethys.

96025.q: What are ophiolites, such as those found in the Grisons?
a: Remnants of old ocean floor that were pushed onto land
Fossilised trees from a primeval forest
Deposits from glaciers of the last ice age
96025.e: Ophiolites consist of rocks of the oceanic crust such as pillow lava and serpentinite. In the Alps they show that the Tethys Ocean once lay here.
96025.m: Ophiolites are pieces of old seabed in the mountains.

96026.q: Geologically speaking, what is the Molasse Basin?
a: a foreland basin north of the Alps
a rift valley like the Upper Rhine Graben
96026.e: Under the weight of the nappes, the European Plate bent downwards in front of the Alps. The debris eroded from the mountains collected in the resulting depression.
96026.m: The Molasse Basin is the debris trough in front of the Alps.

96027.q: Which order of the Molasse groups is correct, from oldest to youngest?
96027.e: The Lower Marine Molasse (LMM) is followed by the Lower Freshwater Molasse (LFM), then the Upper Marine Molasse (UMM) and finally the Upper Freshwater Molasse (UFM). So sea and land alternated twice.
96027.m: In the Molasse, sea and fresh water alternate twice.

96028.q: In which period was the Molasse in the Swiss Plateau mainly deposited?
96028.e: Molasse deposition began about 34 million years ago and lasted into the late Miocene. After that the basin was raised and eroded.
96028.m: The Molasse is a legacy of the Oligocene and Miocene.

96029.q: What is the coarse conglomerate of rounded river pebbles that makes up the Rigi called?
96029.e: Nagelfluh formed in large debris fans where ancient rivers deposited pebbles from the Alps. The pebbles stick out of the rock face like the heads of nails.
96029.m: Nagelfluh is natural concrete made of Alpine pebbles.

96030.q: What is the part of the Molasse Basin at the edge of the Alps that was broken into slices and partly overridden by nappes called?
96030.e: At the southern edge of the basin, the Molasse layers were broken into slices and tilted steeply. Further north they lie almost flat.
96030.m: The Subalpine Molasse is the sliced-up Molasse at the edge of the Alps.

96031.q: Which fossil from Öhningen on the Untersee did the Zurich naturalist Johann Jakob Scheuchzer believe in 1726 to be a human from the Great Flood?
96031.e: Scheuchzer described the skeleton from the Miocene limestones of Öhningen as “Homo diluvii testis”. Georges Cuvier later recognised that it was a giant salamander.
96031.m: The supposed Flood man was a giant salamander.

96032.q: Which sandstone of the Upper Marine Molasse shapes the look of Bern's Old Town and Bern Minster?
96032.e: The grey-green Bernese sandstone was quarried around Bern. It is easy to work but weathers quickly.
96032.m: Bern is built of Molasse sandstone.

96033.q: In the streams of which Molasse upland in the Emmental and Entlebuch is gold still panned today?
96033.e: The Napf is a large debris fan of an ancient Miocene river from the Alps. Its pebbles contain fine gold dust, which collects in the streams.
96033.m: In the Napf area, gold seekers pan gold from Molasse pebbles.

96034.q: When was the Folded Jura mainly folded up?
a: in the late Miocene and Pliocene
96034.e: The folding took place in roughly the last 10 million years as a late result of the formation of the Alps. The rocks themselves are mostly from the Jurassic, but their folding is much younger.
96034.m: The Jura is old rock in young folds.

96035.q: On which layers did the sedimentary cover of the Folded Jura slide off its base?
96035.e: The Triassic evaporites are very soft and formed a sliding layer. The package of layers above it was folded, while the base beneath stayed almost undeformed.
96035.m: The Folded Jura slid together on Triassic salt.

96036.q: According to the distant push hypothesis, where did the pressure that squeezed the Folded Jura together come from?
a: From the Alps in the south
From the Rhine Graben in the north
From the Atlantic in the west
96036.e: The Basel geologist August Buxtorf recognised that the Jura layers had been sheared off above the base. The push came from the distant Alps.
96036.m: According to the distant push hypothesis, the Alps squeezed the Jura together.

96037.q: What is a narrow transverse valley where a river breaks through a Jura ridge, for example near Balsthal, called?
96037.e: The rivers were older than the folding and cut down while the ridges slowly rose. This created gorge-like breakthroughs.
96037.m: A Klus is a river breakthrough right across a Jura ridge.

96038.q: What is the northern, unfolded part of the Jura with almost flat-lying layers called?
96038.e: The Tabular Jura in Aargau and Basel-Landschaft was largely spared from folding. Its layers dip only slightly.
96038.m: In the Tabular Jura the layers lie like table tops.

96039.q: What typically forms the mountain ridges in the Chain Jura?
96039.e: The upward-arching crests of the folds form the ridges, and the downward-arching troughs form the longitudinal valleys. In the Jura the shape of the landscape often matches the folds directly.
96039.m: In the Jura the ridges are fold crests and the valleys are fold troughs.

96040.q: What is the highest peak of the entire Jura mountains called?
96040.e: At 1720 m, the Crêt de la Neige lies in the French Jura north-west of Geneva. The highest Swiss Jura peak is Mont Tendre at 1679 m.
96040.m: The Jura reaches its highest point at the French Crêt de la Neige.

96041.q: Who named rock layers after the Jura mountains in 1795, which later gave rise to the name of the Jurassic period?
96041.e: In 1795 Humboldt used the name Jura for rock layers in the Jura mountains. In 1829 Alexandre Brongniart extended it to the geological period.
96041.m: The Jurassic period is named after the Jura mountains.

96042.q: How did the rock cirque Creux du Van in the Neuchâtel Jura form?
a: through erosion by glaciers and meltwater
96042.e: Ice age glaciers and their meltwater wore away the rock, with softer layers being cleared out faster than hard ones. What remained was a cirque with vertical limestone walls.
96042.m: The Creux du Van is the work of erosion by ice and water.

96043.q: According to the national survey, by roughly how much are parts of the Swiss Alps rising today?
a: up to about 1.5 mm per year
up to about 15 cm per year
up to about 1.5 m per year
up to about 1.5 km per year
96043.e: Repeated precision levelling and GNSS measurements show uplift of just over a millimetre per year in the Central Alps. Over thousands of years this adds up considerably.
96043.m: Today the Alps are growing by about one to one and a half millimetres per year.

96044.q: In which regions of Switzerland is today's uplift greatest?
96044.e: The highest uplift rates are in the Central Alps, especially around Brig and Chur. The Swiss Plateau and the Jura hardly rise at all.
96044.m: The Central Alps in Valais and the Grisons are rising the most.

96045.q: What is the principle called by which the Earth's crust floats in the mantle like an iceberg and rises when a load is removed?
96045.e: When a load such as ice or rock is removed, the lighter crust slowly rises until a new balance is reached. This adjustment contributes to the uplift of the Alps.
96045.m: Isostasy makes crust rise again when a load is removed.

96046.q: According to a 2016 study, which process explains a large part of the uplift of the Alps measured today?
a: the melting of the ice age glaciers
96046.e: After the last ice age the weight of the ice disappeared, and since then the crust has been slowly springing back. The study showed that this effect can explain much of the uplift.
96046.m: The Alps are also rising because the ice age glaciers have disappeared.

96047.q: Why do the Alps not keep getting higher despite the uplift?
a: Because erosion removes about the same amount of rock.
Because the plates are standing still.
96047.e: Rivers, glaciers, rockfalls and weathering remove roughly as much as the mountains rise. Uplift and erosion are therefore roughly in balance.
96047.m: In the Alps, uplift and erosion are roughly in balance.

96048.q: What is the process called by which deeply buried rock returns to the surface through uplift and erosion?
96048.e: During exhumation, rocks from deep down are exposed. This is how high-pressure rocks from many kilometres down reached today's Alps.
96048.m: Exhumation brings deep rock to the light of day.

96049.q: How can you find out when a rock visible today came up from the depths?
a: Using traces of radioactive decay in minerals
By counting annual layers in ice
By measuring the colour of the rock
96049.e: Certain minerals only store traces of radioactive decay once they have cooled below a certain temperature. For apatite this limit is about 100 °C, that is, a few kilometres below the surface.
96049.m: Radioactive traces in minerals reveal when a rock rose.

96050.q: Roughly how thick is the Earth's crust beneath the Central Alps?
96050.e: Beneath the Alps the crust is thickened into a mountain root; beneath the Swiss Plateau it is only about 30 km thick. This light root carries the mountains like a float.
96050.m: Beneath the Alps the crust reaches especially deep.

96051.q: Which two large units does the Insubric Line separate?
96051.e: North of the line lie the strongly transformed nappes of the Central Alps, south of it the Southern Alps. The line is one of the most important faults in the Alps.
96051.m: The Insubric Line separates the Southern Alps from the rest of the Alps.

96052.q: Which larger fault system does the Insubric Line belong to?
96052.e: The Periadriatic Seam runs for about 700 km through the Alps. The section from Piedmont to the Valtellina is called the Insubric Line.
96052.m: The Insubric Line is part of the Periadriatic Seam.

96053.q: Through which Swiss region does the Insubric Line run?
96053.e: The line runs from the Centovalli via Locarno and the Magadino Plain towards the Valtellina. It can be recognised by valley furrows and crushed rocks.
96053.m: The Insubric Line crosses Switzerland in Ticino.

96054.q: Geologically speaking, what is the Insubric Line?
a: A large fault along which blocks of rock were shifted against each other
A glacier flowing right across the Alps
An old Roman road across the Alps
96054.e: Along the Insubric Line the blocks moved against each other sideways and vertically. That is why the rocks there are heavily crushed.
96054.m: The Insubric Line is a large fault in the Alps.

96055.q: How do the rocks south of the Insubric Line differ most from those north of it?
a: They hardly became metamorphic during the formation of the Alps.
They are older than the Earth.
They were completely covered by the sea.
96055.e: The southern block was not buried deep and therefore stayed almost unchanged by the Alpine events. Triassic fossils, for example, are well preserved.
96055.m: South of the Insubric Line the rocks stayed almost untransformed.

96056.q: Which granite body intruded along the Periadriatic Seam about 30 million years ago and builds peaks such as Piz Badile?
96056.e: The Bergell pluton is one of the Periadriatic intrusions of the Oligocene. Its smooth granite walls are famous among climbers.
96056.m: The Bergell Granite is young and linked to the Periadriatic Seam.

96057.q: Why is rock that once lay deep in the Earth's crust found at the Insubric Line?
a: Blocks of rock were raised strongly there
96057.e: Along the fault, blocks of crust were raised steeply and the covering layers were eroded. This brought rocks from great depth to the surface.
96057.m: Uplift and erosion bring deep rock to the surface.

96058.q: Which well-known holiday region in Ticino lies on the Insubric Line?
96058.e: The line runs from the Centovalli via Locarno through the Magadino Plain towards the Valtellina. The straight valley furrows follow the crushed rock of the fault.
96058.m: Near Locarno the Insubric Line crosses Ticino.

96059.q: Which rock are the striking reef mountains of the Dolomites, which grew in the Tethys in the Triassic, made of?
96059.e: In the warm, shallow Tethys, organisms built large limestone reefs in the Triassic. By taking up magnesium they later turned into dolomite rock, which gave the mountains their name.
96059.m: The Dolomites are fossilised reefs of the Tethys.

96060.q: Where does the name “Insubric” come from?
a: from the Celtic people of the Insubres around Milan
from the Latin word for island
96060.e: In ancient times the Insubres lived in the area around Milan. The region at the southern foot of the Alps is also called Insubria after them.
96060.m: The Insubric Line is named after the ancient Insubres.

96061.q: What can be found in the Arosa Zone in the Grisons?
a: Sheared remnants of a former ocean floor
The oldest dinosaur bones in Europe
Young volcanoes from the ice age
Pure salt deposits from an inland sea
96061.e: The Arosa Zone is a mixture of ophiolite and sediment blocks from the South Penninic Ocean. It was sheared beneath the advancing Austroalpine nappes.
96061.m: The Arosa Zone is a sheared piece of ocean floor.

96062.q: What does a negative reaction enthalpy ΔH mean?
96062.e: With ΔH < 0, the system gives off heat to its surroundings. The products are at a lower energy than the reactants.
96062.m: A negative ΔH means that heat is released.

96063.q: What does the reaction enthalpy ΔH of a reaction tell you?
a: the heat taken in or given off at constant pressure
the activation energy of the reaction
96063.e: The reaction enthalpy describes the heat exchanged in a reaction at constant pressure. If it is negative, heat is released; if it is positive, heat is taken in.
96063.m: The reaction enthalpy is the heat a reaction exchanges at constant pressure.

96064.q: What is the standard enthalpy of formation of an element in its most stable form, such as O₂ (g)?
96064.e: Elements in their standard state are the reference point for enthalpies of formation. Their value is therefore set to zero by definition.
96064.m: Pure elements in their standard state have an enthalpy of formation of zero.

96065.q: The standard enthalpy of formation of liquid water is about −286 kJ/mol. What does this mean?
a: When 1 mol of water forms from H₂ and O₂, about 286 kJ is released.
When 1 mol of water forms, about 286 kJ is taken in.
Water breaks down into its elements at 286 °C.
1 mol of water contains 286 kJ of kinetic energy.
96065.e: The negative sign shows that energy is released. So the formation of water from hydrogen and oxygen is strongly exothermic, as the oxyhydrogen reaction shows.
96065.m: The formation of liquid water releases about 286 kJ per mole.

96066.q: What is ΔH for CH₄ + 2 O₂ → CO₂ + 2 H₂O (l) if ΔfH(CH₄) = −74.8, ΔfH(CO₂) = −393.5 and ΔfH(H₂O, l) = −285.8 kJ/mol?
96066.e: ΔH = sum of products minus sum of reactants = (−393.5 + 2·(−285.8)) − (−74.8) = −965.1 + 74.8 = −890.3 kJ/mol. As an element, O₂ has the value zero.
96066.m: The reaction enthalpy is the sum of the enthalpies of formation of the products minus that of the reactants.

96067.q: What is ΔH for H₂ + Cl₂ → 2 HCl if the bond enthalpies are H-H 436, Cl-Cl 242 and H-Cl 431 kJ/mol?
96067.e: Breaking the bonds takes 436 + 242 = 678 kJ, and forming them releases 2·431 = 862 kJ. ΔH = 678 − 862 = −184 kJ/mol.
96067.m: Breaking bonds costs energy, forming bonds releases energy.

96068.q: Which device is used in the laboratory to measure the heat released in a reaction?
96068.e: In the calorimeter, the reaction takes place in a well-insulated vessel. The heat exchanged is calculated from the change in temperature of the water.
96068.m: Heats of reaction are measured with a calorimeter.

96069.q: Why does it take much less energy to melt ice than to boil away the same amount of water?
a: When ice melts, only some of the hydrogen bonds break.
When ice melts, the O-H bonds in the molecule are split.
When water boils, it is split into hydrogen and oxygen.
96069.e: In liquid water, the molecules are still held together by many hydrogen bonds. Only when it evaporates do they have to be separated completely, which takes about seven times more energy.
96069.m: Melting takes much less energy than evaporating.

96070.q: In Ludwig Boltzmann's sense, what does entropy measure?
a: the bond strength in a molecule
96070.e: According to Boltzmann, S = k·ln W, where W is the number of microstates. The more arrangements are possible, the greater the entropy.
96070.m: Many possible arrangements mean high entropy.

96071.q: In which unit is molar entropy given?
96071.e: Entropy is heat divided by temperature, so joules per kelvin, per mole. That is why standard entropies are listed in tables in J/(mol·K).
96071.m: Molar entropies are measured in joules per mole and kelvin.

96072.q: What does the second law of thermodynamics say about an isolated system?
a: Its temperature always stays the same.
96072.e: In an isolated system, processes happen spontaneously only in such a way that the total entropy increases or stays the same. That is why heat only flows by itself from warm to cold.
96072.m: In an isolated system, entropy increases or stays the same.

96073.q: What does the third law of thermodynamics state?
a: A perfect crystal has zero entropy at 0 K.
At 0 K the enthalpy is at its maximum.
Every reaction is exothermic at 0 K.
Gases have the greatest entropy at 0 K.
96073.e: At absolute zero, an ideal crystal has only one single microstate. It follows that S = k·ln 1 = 0, which makes absolute entropy values possible.
96073.m: A perfect crystal at absolute zero has no entropy.

96074.q: In which reaction does the entropy of the system increase markedly?
96074.e: A solid produces a solid and a gas. Gases have very many more microstates, so the entropy rises strongly.
96074.m: If extra gas forms in a reaction, the entropy usually increases.

96075.q: What is the entropy of vaporisation of water at its boiling point if ΔH_V = 40.7 kJ/mol?
96075.e: At a phase change, ΔS = ΔH/T = 40,700 J/mol / 373 K ≈ 109 J/(mol·K). Because of the hydrogen bonds, the value is larger than for many other liquids.
96075.m: At a phase change, the change in entropy equals enthalpy divided by temperature.

96076.q: Why is the entropy of vaporisation of water greater than for most other liquids?
a: Hydrogen bonds order the molecules in liquid water especially strongly.
Water has an especially large molecular mass.
Water vapour is more ordered than liquid water.
Water boils at an especially low temperature.
96076.e: Liquid water is more strongly ordered by hydrogen bonds than other liquids. When it evaporates, this order is lost, so the entropy increases especially strongly.
96076.m: Hydrogen bonds make liquid water especially ordered.

96077.q: Which physicist introduced the term entropy in 1865?
96077.e: Rudolf Clausius formed the word from the Greek for “transformation”. For some years he also taught at the Polytechnic in Zurich, today's ETH.
96077.m: Rudolf Clausius gave entropy its name.

96078.q: Which equation gives the Gibbs free energy change ΔG from ΔH and ΔS?
96078.e: Gibbs energy links enthalpy and entropy. The entropy term becomes more important the higher the temperature.
96078.m: Gibbs free energy is enthalpy minus temperature times entropy.

96079.q: When does a reaction take place spontaneously at constant pressure and temperature?
a: when ΔG is less than zero
when ΔG is greater than zero
when ΔH is greater than zero
96079.e: A reaction with ΔG < 0 is called exergonic and can happen by itself. However, ΔG says nothing about the rate.
96079.m: Exergonic reactions with a negative ΔG happen spontaneously.

96080.q: Which reaction is spontaneous at every temperature?
96080.e: With ΔH < 0 and ΔS > 0, both terms in ΔG = ΔH − T·ΔS are negative. So ΔG is always less than zero.
96080.m: Exothermic with an increase in entropy is always spontaneous.

96081.q: From what temperature does CaCO₃ break down spontaneously into CaO and CO₂ if ΔH = +178 kJ/mol and ΔS = +161 J/(mol·K)?
96081.e: ΔG becomes zero at T = ΔH/ΔS = 178,000 / 161 ≈ 1,106 K, so about 830 °C. Above that the entropy term dominates, which is why lime is burnt in hot kilns.
96081.m: Endothermic reactions with an increase in entropy only become spontaneous at high temperature.

96082.q: What is the value of the equilibrium constant K if ΔG° of a reaction is exactly zero?
96082.e: ΔG° = −R·T·ln K. If ΔG° = 0, then ln K = 0 and so K = 1.
96082.m: When ΔG° equals zero, the equilibrium constant is one.

96083.q: Roughly what is K at 298 K if ΔG° = −5.7 kJ/mol and R = 8.314 J/(mol·K)?
96083.m: The more negative ΔG°, the larger the equilibrium constant.

96084.q: What is ΔG° for N₂ + 3 H₂ → 2 NH₃ at 298 K if ΔH° = −92.2 kJ and ΔS° = −198.7 J/K?
96084.e: ΔG° = −92.2 kJ − 298 K · (−0.1987 kJ/K) = −92.2 + 59.2 ≈ −33 kJ. The decrease in entropy clearly weakens the enthalpy gain.
96084.m: A decrease in entropy makes ΔG less negative than ΔH.

96085.q: What kind of scientist is Gibbs energy named after?
96085.e: Josiah Willard Gibbs from New Haven developed chemical thermodynamics in the 19th century. Gibbs free energy G bears his name.
96085.m: Gibbs energy honours the American Josiah Willard Gibbs.

a: The reaction enthalpy does not depend on the reaction path.
The reaction rate doubles for every 10 K.
The entropy of a crystal is zero at 0 K.
96086.e: Whether a reaction happens in one step or via intermediate stages, the total change in enthalpy stays the same. That is why partial reactions can be added together.
96086.m: The change in enthalpy depends only on the start and the end.

96087.q: In which city was Germain Henri Hess born in 1802?
96087.e: Hess was born in Geneva and grew up in Russia, where he did research in Saint Petersburg. In 1840 he formulated the law named after him.
96087.m: Hess, the founder of thermochemistry, came from Geneva.

96088.q: What is ΔH for C + ½ O₂ → CO if C + O₂ → CO₂ has ΔH = −393.5 kJ/mol and CO + ½ O₂ → CO₂ has ΔH = −283.0 kJ/mol?
96088.e: You take the first equation and subtract the second: −393.5 − (−283.0) = −110.5 kJ/mol. This gives a value that can hardly be measured directly.
96088.m: With Hess's law, you calculate unknown enthalpies from known partial steps.

96089.q: Why can the enthalpy of formation of CO hardly be measured directly in a calorimeter?
a: Because CO₂ is always formed as well when carbon burns.
Because CO is a solid at room temperature.
96089.e: Carbon never burns cleanly to CO alone; a mixture with CO₂ forms. That is why the value is calculated using a Hess cycle.
96089.m: What cannot be measured directly is worked out by a roundabout route.

96090.q: What sign does ΔH get when you reverse a chemical equation?
96090.e: The reverse reaction uses exactly as much energy as the forward reaction releases, or the other way round. The size stays the same and the sign changes.
96090.m: If you turn the equation round, you must turn round the sign of ΔH.

96091.q: What is ΔH for 2 H₂O (l) → 2 H₂ + O₂ if H₂ + ½ O₂ → H₂O (l) has ΔH = −286 kJ?
96091.e: The equation is reversed, giving +286 kJ, and multiplied by 2. That gives +572 kJ.
96091.m: If you double an equation, you also double ΔH.

96092.q: Which property of enthalpy is Hess's law based on?
96092.e: State functions depend only on the current state, not on the path taken to get there. Work and heat on their own, on the other hand, depend on the path.
96092.m: Because enthalpy is a state function, only the start and the finish count.

96093.q: Which cycle uses Hess's law to determine the lattice energy of ionic crystals?
96093.e: In the Born-Haber cycle, sublimation, ionisation, electron affinity and enthalpy of formation are combined. The lattice energy is the missing link.
96093.m: The Born-Haber cycle calculates lattice energies via partial steps.

96094.q: What is ΔH for graphite → diamond if the enthalpies of combustion are −393.5 kJ/mol for graphite and −395.4 kJ/mol for diamond?
96094.e: Burn graphite to CO₂ and turn CO₂ back into diamond: −393.5 + 395.4 = +1.9 kJ/mol. So diamond is at a slightly higher energy than graphite.
96094.m: Diamond is at a slightly higher energy than graphite.

96095.q: Roughly what is the specific heat capacity of liquid water?
96095.e: Heating 1 g of water by 1 K takes about 4.18 J. This high value makes water the ideal liquid for a calorimeter.
96095.m: Water needs about 4.18 joules per gram and kelvin.

96096.q: How much heat do 200 g of water take in if they warm up by 5 K?
96096.e: Q = m·c·ΔT = 200 g · 4.18 J/(g·K) · 5 K = 4,180 J ≈ 4.2 kJ. This is how the heat released is determined in a calorimeter.
96096.m: Heat is mass times specific heat capacity times change in temperature.

96097.q: What is a bomb calorimeter typically used for?
a: To find the calorific value of foods or fuels
To test the pressure of gas cylinders
To measure the density of metals
96097.e: The sample is burnt completely with oxygen in a sealed steel container. The energy released is calculated from how much the surrounding water warms up.
96097.m: A bomb calorimeter measures the calorific value of a substance.

96098.q: What is the amount of heat that the calorimeter itself takes in per kelvin of temperature rise called?
96098.e: The vessel, stirrer and thermometer also take in heat. This heat capacity is determined beforehand and taken into account in the calculation.
96098.m: The calorimeter constant accounts for the heat the device itself absorbs.

96099.q: 50 mL of HCl (1 mol/L) and 50 mL of NaOH (1 mol/L) warm up by 6.8 K when mixed. Roughly what is the enthalpy of neutralisation?
96099.e: Q = 100 g · 4.18 J/(g·K) · 6.8 K ≈ 2,842 J for the formation of 0.05 mol of water. 2,842 J / 0.05 mol ≈ 57 kJ/mol, released, so negative.
96099.m: Neutralising strong acids with strong bases releases about 57 kJ per mole of water.

96100.q: Which double-walled, evacuated vessel prevents heat loss in the calorimeter?
96100.e: The vacuum between the walls stops heat conduction and convection. A mirrored inner wall also reduces heat radiation.
96100.m: A Dewar flask keeps the heat in the calorimeter.

96101.q: How does the gross calorific value of a fuel differ from the net calorific value?
a: The gross value includes the heat of condensation of the water.
The gross value only applies to solid fuels.
The net value is always larger than the gross value.
The net value takes exhaust gas cleaning into account.
96101.e: For the gross calorific value, the water produced is counted as a liquid; for the net value, as steam. Condensing boilers use this extra heat.
96101.m: The gross calorific value is larger than the net value by the heat of condensation.

96102.q: Which two researchers built an ice calorimeter in the 1780s?
96102.e: Antoine Lavoisier and Pierre-Simon Laplace measured amounts of heat by the amount of ice that melted. In this way they also measured the heat given off by a guinea pig.
96102.m: Lavoisier and Laplace measured heat with melting ice.

96103.q: How is the rate of reaction defined?
a: Change in concentration per unit of time
96103.e: You measure how fast the concentration of a reactant falls or of a product rises. The unit is usually mol/(L·s).
96103.m: The rate of reaction tells you how fast concentrations change.

96104.q: According to collision theory, which two conditions does a collision need to lead to a reaction?
a: enough energy and the right orientation
the same charge and the same size
96104.e: Products only form if the particles collide with at least the activation energy and in a favourable orientation. Most collisions have no effect.
96104.m: Only energetic, correctly oriented collisions are effective.

96105.q: What is the highest-energy state on the reaction path between reactants and products called?
96105.e: At the transition state, old bonds are broken and new ones formed. Its energy above the reactants equals the activation energy.
96105.m: The transition state is the peak of the energy profile.

96106.q: Why does zinc powder react faster with hydrochloric acid than a lump of zinc of the same mass?
a: It has a larger surface area.
It has a lower activation energy.
It is more noble than the lump.
96106.e: Reactions with solids take place at the surface. The more finely divided it is, the more particles can be hit at the same time.
96106.m: More finely divided means more surface area and a faster reaction.

96107.q: In a multi-step reaction, which step determines the overall rate?
96107.e: Like a bottleneck, the slowest partial step limits the speed of the whole reaction. It is called the rate-determining step.
96107.m: The slowest step sets the pace of the whole reaction.

96108.q: What does the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution show when the temperature rises?
a: More particles exceed the activation energy.
All particles have the same energy.
96108.e: At higher temperature, the energy distribution shifts to higher values. The share of particles with enough energy grows strongly.
96108.m: Heat increases the share of particles able to react.

96109.q: As a rule of thumb, what does the van 't Hoff rule (RGT rule) say?
a: For 10 K more, the rate rises two to four times.
For 10 K more, the rate halves.
For 100 K more, the rate stays the same.
For 1 K more, the rate increases tenfold.
96109.e: This reaction rate and temperature rule goes back to van 't Hoff. It only applies roughly, and for many reactions near room temperature.
96109.m: Ten degrees warmer makes many reactions two to four times faster.

96110.q: What is the general form of the rate law for a reaction A + B → products?
96110.e: The rate is proportional to powers of the concentrations. The proportionality factor k is called the rate constant.
96110.m: The rate constant links concentrations with the rate of reaction.

96111.q: What unit does the rate constant of a first-order reaction have?
96111.e: With v = k·c, v has the unit mol/(L·s) and c the unit mol/L. So k is left with 1/s.
96111.m: For first order, k has the unit per second.

96112.q: What unit does the rate constant of a second-order reaction have?
96112.e: With v = k·c², k = v/c² with (mol/(L·s)) / (mol/L)². That gives L/(mol·s).
96112.m: For second order, k has the unit litres per mole and second.

96113.q: What does the rate constant k of a reaction NOT depend on?
96113.e: For a reaction at a given temperature, k is constant. The concentrations appear separately in the rate law.
96113.m: Concentrations change v, but not k.

96114.q: What is the half-life of a first-order reaction with k = 0.0231 min⁻¹?
96114.e: For first order, t½ = ln 2 / k = 0.693 / 0.0231 min⁻¹ = 30 min. So the half-life depends only on k.
96114.m: For first order, the half-life is ln 2 divided by k.

96115.q: What is v for a first-order reaction with k = 0.05 s⁻¹ at c = 0.2 mol/L?
96115.e: v = k·c = 0.05 s⁻¹ · 0.2 mol/L = 0.01 mol/(L·s). If the concentration halves, v halves too.
96115.m: For first order, v equals k times the concentration.

96116.q: How is the equilibrium constant K related to the rate constants of the forward and reverse reactions?
96116.e: At equilibrium, the forward and reverse reactions are equally fast. For elementary reactions, it follows that K is the ratio of the two constants.
96116.m: The equilibrium constant is the ratio of the rate constants.

96117.q: What is v for v = k·c(A)·c(B) with k = 2 L/(mol·s) and c(A) = c(B) = 0.1 mol/L?
96117.e: v = 2 L/(mol·s) · 0.1 mol/L · 0.1 mol/L = 0.02 mol/(L·s). The units cancel down to mol/(L·s).
96117.m: You simply put k and the concentrations into the rate law.

96118.q: How is the overall order of a reaction with v = k·c(A)²·c(B) defined, and what is it?
96118.e: The overall order is the sum of all the exponents in the rate law. Here 2 + 1 gives a third-order reaction.
96118.m: The overall order is the sum of the exponents.

96119.q: How is the order of a reaction reliably determined?
a: from the coefficients of the equation
from the molar mass of the reactants
96119.e: In multi-step reactions, the exponents often do not match the stoichiometric coefficients. This is only the case for elementary reactions.
96119.m: Reaction orders have to be measured, not read off the equation.

96120.q: What is special about the half-life of a first-order reaction?
a: It does not depend on the starting concentration.
It is always exactly one second.
96120.e: With first order, it always takes the same time for half to be converted, no matter how much there was at the start. With second order, on the other hand, it gets longer.
96120.m: For first order, the half-life stays constant.

96121.q: Which process follows a first-order rate law?
96121.e: Each nucleus decays independently with the same probability, so the decay rate is proportional to the number of nuclei. That is exactly first order.
96121.m: Radioactive decay is the textbook example of first order.

96122.q: If you double c(A), the rate of reaction quadruples. What is the order of the reaction with respect to A?
96122.e: v ∝ c(A)^n with 2^n = 4. It follows that n = 2.
96122.m: If v quadruples when the concentration doubles, the order is two.

96123.q: Approximately what is the order of the breakdown of alcohol in the liver?
96123.e: The enzyme is already working at full capacity with small amounts of alcohol. So about the same amount is broken down each hour, regardless of concentration.
96123.m: A saturated enzyme works in zero order at a constant pace.

96124.q: For a first-order reaction, which plot gives a straight line?
96124.e: From ln c = ln c₀ − k·t you get a straight line with gradient −k. For second order, on the other hand, 1/c against t is linear.
96124.m: For first order, ln c lies on a straight line over time.

96125.q: In a first-order reaction, what percentage of a reactant is still present after three half-lives?
96125.e: After each half-life the remainder halves: 100 % → 50 % → 25 % → 12.5 %. (½)³ = 1/8.
96125.m: After three half-lives, one eighth is left.

96126.q: In a hydrolysis, water is present in huge excess. How does the water concentration behave during the reaction?
a: It swings wildly up and down
96126.e: Only a tiny part of the water is used up. The reaction then depends only on the concentration of the other partner and behaves like a first-order reaction.
96126.m: A large excess of one partner keeps its concentration almost constant.

96127.q: What does the Arrhenius equation describe?
a: How the rate of reaction depends on temperature
How gas pressure depends on volume
How much heat a reaction releases
How strongly an acid dissociates in water
96127.e: The Arrhenius equation links the rate constant with temperature and activation energy. The higher the temperature, the faster the reaction.
96127.m: The Arrhenius equation links rate of reaction, temperature and activation energy.

96128.q: Which Swedish chemist described in 1889, with an equation, how the rate of reaction depends on temperature?
96128.e: Svante Arrhenius published the equation named after him in 1889. He received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1903, mainly for his theory of electrolytic dissociation.
96128.m: Svante Arrhenius described how the rate of reaction depends on temperature.

96129.q: Why do most reactions go faster at higher temperature?
a: More particles have enough energy to overcome the activation energy
The equilibrium then always lies with the products
96129.e: At higher temperature the particles move faster. A larger share of the collisions has enough energy for a reaction.
96129.m: Heat gives more particles enough energy for a successful reaction.

96130.q: Which quantity can be determined by measuring the rate of a reaction at different temperatures?
96130.e: If you plot ln k against 1/T, you get a straight line. The activation energy can be calculated from its gradient.
96130.m: Measurements at different temperatures reveal the activation energy.

96131.q: According to the van 't Hoff rule (RGT rule), by roughly what factor does a reaction speed up when the temperature rises by 10 °C?
96131.e: This reaction rate and temperature rule is a rule of thumb. Many reactions become about two to four times as fast for every 10 °C.
96131.m: For every 10 degrees more, many reactions run about two to four times faster.

96132.q: Which reactions are especially sensitive to a change in temperature?
a: those with a high activation energy
those with a low activation energy
96132.e: The larger Ea, the steeper the line in the Arrhenius plot. Then k changes more for the same change in temperature.
96132.m: High activation energy means strong dependence on temperature.

96133.q: How does a catalyst speed up a chemical reaction?
a: It shifts the equilibrium towards the products
96133.e: The catalyst makes another reaction path with a lower activation energy possible. Just 10 kJ/mol less makes a reaction at room temperature about 50 times faster.
96133.m: A small reduction in activation energy speeds up reactions enormously.

96134.q: A reaction takes eight minutes at 20 °C. How long does it take at 40 °C if the rate doubles for every 10 °C?
96134.e: From 20 °C to 40 °C the rate doubles twice, so it becomes four times as fast. 8 minutes divided by 4 gives 2 minutes.
96134.m: The van 't Hoff rule lets you estimate how heat speeds up a reaction.

96135.q: In the esterification of acetic acid with ethanol, how do you increase the yield of ester?
a: by using an excess of ethanol
96135.e: More reactant shifts the equilibrium towards the products. Water, on the other hand, would favour the reverse reaction.
96135.m: An excess of reactant drives the equilibrium towards the products.

96136.q: What is the effect of continuously removing a product from an equilibrium mixture?
96136.e: The system makes up for the loss by forming more product. K stays the same; only the concentrations adjust.
96136.m: Removing products gets more of them out of the equilibrium.

96137.q: The equilibrium N₂O₄ (colourless) ⇌ 2 NO₂ (brown) is endothermic in the forward direction. What happens when it is heated?
96137.e: Heat acts like a reactant of the endothermic forward reaction. More brown NO₂ is formed.

96362.q: On which day does spring usually begin according to the calendar?
96362.e: According to the calendar, spring usually begins on 20 or 21 March. From then on, the midday sun is a little higher each day.

96363.q: Roughly how long are day and night at the start of spring?
96363.e: At the start of spring, day and night last almost exactly the same time, about 12 hours each. This day is also called the equinox.
96363.m: At the start of spring, day and night are about the same length.

96364.q: What happens to the days in spring?
96364.e: In spring the sun rises a little earlier and sets a little later each day. So the days get longer and plants get more light.
96364.m: In spring the days get longer.

96365.q: On which day does spring begin for weather experts?
96365.e: Weather experts count in whole months. For them, spring lasts from 1 March to the end of May.
96365.m: For weather experts, spring begins on 1 March.

96366.q: Which Zurich festival drives away winter by burning the “Böögg”?
96366.e: At Sechseläuten in Zurich, a snowman made of cotton wool, the Böögg, is burnt. It stands for the winter, which should leave.
96366.m: At Sechseläuten in Zurich the Böögg is burnt.

96367.q: Which bird comes back from Africa in spring and is seen as a sign of spring?
96367.e: Swallows spend the winter in Africa. When they come back in spring, there are lots of insects for them again.
96367.m: The swallow is a sign of spring.

96368.q: Why do plants start growing again in spring?
96368.e: Plants need warmth and light to grow. In spring the sun shines for longer and the ground thaws.
96368.m: Warmth and light wake up the plants in spring.

96369.q: What rises up inside tree trunks in spring?
96369.e: In spring the roots take up water again. This sap rises with nutrients right up to the buds.
96369.m: In spring the sap rises in the trees.

96370.q: What do a tree's new leaves grow out of in spring?
96370.e: The leaves are already hidden, tiny, in the buds. In spring the buds open and the leaves grow out.
96370.m: New leaves grow out of buds.

96371.q: What colour are very young leaves in spring usually?
96371.e: Young leaves are delicate and still have little chlorophyll. That is why they shine light green in spring.

96373.q: Which of these trees is one of the first to get its leaves in spring?
96373.e: In Switzerland the horse chestnut often comes into leaf as early as April. Oak, ash and walnut take their time.
96373.m: The horse chestnut comes into leaf early.

96374.q: Which conifer gets completely new, light green needles every spring?
96374.e: The larch is a conifer that grows new needles every year. In spring they are soft and light green.
96374.m: The larch gets new needles every spring.

96375.q: What makes the buds open in spring?
96375.e: When it has been warm enough for a while, the buds start to swell. Then they open and the leaves come out.

96376.q: How do the young leaves lie inside the bud?
96376.e: There is not much room in the bud. That is why the leaves are tightly folded or rolled, and unfold as they come out.
96376.m: Inside the bud, the leaves are tightly folded.

96378.q: Which low spring flower often forms purple and white carpets in meadows?
96378.e: The crocus flowers in March with purple, white or yellow flowers. It has only a very short stalk.
96378.m: The crocus flowers early in the year in the meadows.

96379.q: Where do many early spring flowers store their food?
a: In the seeds on the stalk
96379.e: Early spring flowers have food stored under the ground. This lets them grow quickly even when it is still cool.
96379.m: Early spring flowers have food stores in bulbs or tubers.

96380.q: Why do wood anemones in the forest flower so early?
a: The trees have no leaves yet
The forest is hotter in spring
There are no bees in summer
96380.e: In spring, lots of light falls on the forest floor because the trees are still bare. Later it is too shady there.
96380.m: Early flowers in the forest use the light before the leaves come.

96381.q: Which yellow spring flower has a flower like a trumpet?
96381.e: The daffodil is a narcissus. In the middle of its flower there is a long tube like a trumpet.
96381.m: The daffodil has a flower like a trumpet.

96382.q: Which spring flower is famous in the Netherlands and planted there in huge fields?
96382.e: The tulip originally comes from Asia. In the Netherlands, huge colourful tulip fields bloom in spring.
96382.m: The tulip is famous in the Netherlands.

96384.e: The cowslip has yellow flowers in spring. Several flowers hang from one stalk like a bunch of keys.

96385.q: The squill is a small blue flower with star-shaped flowers. When does it flower?
96385.e: The squill, also called Scilla, flowers in March and April. It is one of the early spring flowers.

96387.q: Which fruit tree usually flowers before the apple tree in spring?
96387.e: Here, cherry trees often flower as early as April. The apple trees follow a little later.
96387.m: The cherry tree flowers before the apple tree.

96388.q: What falls from the fruit trees like snow after they have flowered?
96388.e: When flowering is over, the petals fall off. They then lie under the tree like snow.
96388.m: After flowering, the petals fall off.

96389.q: In which country do people celebrate the cherry blossom with big festivals under the trees?
96389.e: In Japan, lots of people sit under the flowering cherry trees in spring. This festival is called Hanami.

96390.q: Which shrub flowers as early as February and lets yellow catkins dangle in the wind?
96390.e: The hazel flowers very early in the year, even before its leaves. Its long yellow catkins release lots of pollen.
96390.m: The hazel flowers as early as February.

96391.q: Which tree do the soft, silvery “palm catkins” come from?
96391.e: The goat willow forms soft, silvery catkins in March. They are an important first food for bees.
96391.m: Palm catkins grow on the willow.

96392.q: What can a late frost do while the trees are in flower?
96392.e: Frozen blossoms can no longer form fruit. That is why there is less fruit after a frost during flowering.
96392.m: Frost can freeze the blossoms on trees.

96393.q: What does the wind carry from birch flowers to other birches?
96393.e: Birches are pollinated by the wind. The fine dust from the flowers is called pollen, and some people get hay fever from it.
96393.m: The wind carries birch pollen further.

96394.q: Which tree flowers in early summer, smells sweet and attracts lots of bees?
96394.e: The lime tree flowers in June and July. Its flowers smell strongly, and they are also used to make lime blossom tea.
96394.m: The lime tree flowers in summer and smells sweet.

96395.q: Which big yellow flower turns towards the sun when it is a young plant?
96395.e: Young sunflowers follow the sun from east to west during the day. Once fully grown, their flowers usually face east.
96395.m: The young sunflower follows the sun.

96396.q: Which red flower often grows in summer at the edge of cornfields?
96396.e: The common poppy has thin, bright red petals. It likes to grow at the edges of fields and on fallow land.
96396.m: The poppy flowers red by the cornfield.

96397.q: Which blue flower gets its name from the cornfield?
96397.e: In the past, the cornflower often grew among the cereal crops, in the corn. It flowers bright blue in summer.
96397.m: The cornflower is named after the cornfield.

96398.q: Which alpine flower is deep blue and has flowers like little funnels?
96398.e: The gentian grows in mountain meadows and has bright blue flowers. Its flowers are shaped like little bells or funnels.
96398.m: The gentian flowers deep blue in the mountains.

96399.q: Which summer flower has orange flowers that you can even eat?
96399.e: The nasturtium flowers orange, yellow or red all summer. Its flowers and leaves taste peppery and go into salads.

96400.q: Which shrub turns whole slopes red to pink in the Swiss Alps in summer?
96400.e: The alpine rose is a small shrub in the mountains. It flowers a strong pinkish red in June and July.
96400.m: The alpine rose flowers red in the Alps.

96401.q: Which summer plant has lilac flowers and smells so strong that people fill scented bags with it?
96401.e: Lavender flowers purple in summer. Its dried flowers keep their scent for a long time and are often put in little bags.
96401.m: Lavender smells strong and has lilac flowers.

96402.q: Which orange summer flower is used to make an ointment for the skin?
96402.e: The pot marigold flowers from June into autumn. Its flowers are used for a healing skin ointment.
96402.m: Ointment is made from pot marigolds.

96403.q: In which season are most apples harvested?
96403.e: Apples need the whole summer to ripen. Most varieties are picked in September and October.

96404.q: Which festival do many people celebrate in autumn to give thanks for the harvest?
96404.e: At harvest festival, fruit and vegetables are often brought to church. People give thanks for everything that has grown.
96404.m: At harvest festival people give thanks for the harvest.

96406.q: When is cereal such as wheat usually harvested in Switzerland?
96406.e: Wheat is ripe in July and August. Then the ears are golden yellow and dry.
96406.m: Cereal crops are harvested in summer.

96407.q: Which big machine harvests cereal crops in the field?
96407.e: The combine harvester cuts the crop and at the same time separates the grains from the straw. It combines both jobs, which is where its name comes from.
96407.m: The combine harvester harvests the cereal.

96408.q: Which big, often orange vegetable is harvested in autumn and hollowed out at Halloween?
96408.e: Pumpkins grow all through the summer. In autumn they are ripe and are harvested.
96408.m: The pumpkin is harvested in autumn.

96409.q: What do farmers cut in the meadow in summer and dry as food for the winter?
96409.e: Dried grass is called hay. Farmers feed it to their cows in winter, when nothing grows outside.
96409.m: Hay is dried grass for the winter.

96411.q: Which fruits are gathered in Ticino in autumn and sold as hot “marroni”?
96411.e: The sweet chestnut grows mainly on the southern side of the Alps. Its roasted fruits are called marroni.

96412.q: Which tree is on the flag of Canada and famous for its red autumn leaves?
96412.e: The flag of Canada has a red maple leaf on it. In Canada, whole maple forests glow red in autumn.
96412.m: The red maple leaf is on the flag of Canada.

96413.q: What colour do birch leaves turn in autumn?
96413.e: The birch turns bright golden yellow in autumn. Its white bark and yellow leaves are easy to recognise.
96413.m: The birch turns yellow in autumn.

96414.q: Which conifer turns golden yellow in autumn?
96414.e: The larch is a special conifer. In autumn its needles turn golden yellow, for example in the Engadine.
96414.m: The larch turns golden yellow in autumn.

96415.q: Why can you not see the yellow colour in a leaf in summer?
96415.e: The yellow pigments are already in the leaf in summer. Only when the green disappears do they show.
96415.m: In summer the green hides the yellow colour.

96416.q: In which weather do autumn colours become especially bright?
96416.e: Lots of sun during the day and cool nights make some leaves produce lots of red pigment. Then the forest glows especially brightly.
96416.m: Sun and cool nights make autumn colourful.

96417.q: What colour are beech leaves often in late autumn?
96417.e: In autumn, beech leaves first turn yellow and then orange to copper brown. A beech forest then glows warmly.
96417.m: Beech leaves turn copper brown in autumn.

96418.q: Which climbing plant on house walls turns bright red in autumn?
96418.e: Virginia creeper climbs up walls. In autumn its leaves turn deep red and then fall off.
96418.m: Virginia creeper turns red in autumn.

96419.q: Which plants turn the vineyards by Lake Geneva yellow and red in autumn?
96419.e: After the grape harvest, the vine leaves change colour. The vineyards of Lavaux then glow yellow and red.
96419.m: In autumn the vines turn colourful.

96420.q: Where is the best place to put the leaves from the garden?
96420.e: On the compost heap, the leaves break down over time. That way they become good garden soil again.
96420.m: Leaves belong on the compost heap.

96421.q: What does the tree form at the leaf stalk so that the leaf falls off?
96421.e: A thin separation layer grows between the twig and the leaf stalk. Then a gust of wind is enough and the leaf falls off.
96421.m: A separation layer makes the leaf fall off.

96423.q: Which animals pull leaves into the ground and eat them?
96423.e: Earthworms pull leaves into their tunnels and eat them. Their droppings make the soil fertile.

96424.q: Which animal likes to crawl into a pile of leaves to hibernate?
96424.e: A pile of leaves is warm and sheltered. That is why you should leave a few piles of leaves in the garden in autumn.
96424.m: The hedgehog likes to sleep in a pile of leaves.

96425.q: What is the small mark on a twig where a leaf has fallen off called?
96425.e: Where a leaf has fallen off, a small scar is left. It is sealed with a layer of cork.
96425.m: After leaf fall, a leaf scar is left.

96426.q: Which young tree often keeps its dry, brown leaves until spring?
96426.e: Young beeches often only drop their dry leaves in spring. That is why you see brown leaves on small beeches in winter.
96426.m: Young beeches often keep their leaves in winter.

96427.q: What are trees that only have leaves in the summer half of the year called?
96427.e: Deciduous trees such as beech or maple have leaves in summer. In winter they stand bare.
96427.m: Trees that lose their leaves in autumn are deciduous.

96428.q: When does a tree form the buds for the next year?
96428.e: The buds form as early as summer. In autumn and winter they wait, ready, on the twig for spring.
96428.m: The buds already grow in summer.

96429.q: What can you tell from a tree's buds in winter?
a: What kind of tree it is
96429.e: Each kind of tree has buds with their own shape and colour. That is why you can identify trees even without leaves.
96429.m: You can tell the kind of tree from its buds.

96430.q: On which tree do the buds sit in clusters at the tip of the twigs?
96430.e: On the oak, several buds sit close together at the end of a twig. That is a good way to recognise it.
96430.m: The oak has clusters of buds at the end of its twigs.

96431.q: Which tree has black winter buds?
96431.e: In winter, the ash is easy to recognise by its velvety black buds. That is rare among our trees.

96432.q: What is inside a winter bud?
a: A small shoot with leaves or flowers
A seed for a new plant
96432.e: The new shoot is already fully formed inside the bud. In spring it only has to grow and unfold.
96432.m: The new shoot is inside the bud.

96433.q: Which tree has long, pointed, brown buds?
96433.e: Beech buds are long, thin and pointed like little spears. They are light brown.
96433.m: The beech has long, pointed buds.

96434.q: Which branches are cut on 4 December so that they flower in a vase at Christmas?
96434.e: On St Barbara's Day, people cut cherry branches, for example, and put them in water. In the warm living room the buds open by Christmas.
96434.m: St Barbara's branches flower at Christmas.

96435.q: How can you recognise the flower buds on a fruit tree?
96435.e: Flower buds are usually fatter and rounder than leaf buds. They contain the flowers for spring.
96435.m: Flower buds are fatter than leaf buds.

96436.q: What does it mean when a plant is “evergreen”?
a: It has green leaves all year round
It loses all its leaves every autumn
96436.e: Evergreen plants have green leaves or needles in winter too. They replace old leaves bit by bit.
96436.m: Evergreen plants are green all year round.

96437.q: Which conifer has red fruits but very poisonous needles and seeds?
96437.e: The yew is evergreen and grows slowly. Its needles and seeds are very poisonous, for horses too.

96438.q: Which evergreen shrub has prickly leaves and red berries?
96438.e: Holly has shiny, prickly leaves. Its red berries are poisonous to people.
96438.m: Holly has prickly leaves and red berries.

96439.q: Which climbing plant stays green in winter too?
96439.e: Ivy climbs up trees and walls. Its dark green leaves stay on in winter too.

96440.q: Fir needles have a thin layer of wax. What does it protect the needles from in winter?
96440.e: A layer of wax on the needles lets little water escape. That way the tree does not dry out in winter.
96440.m: The wax layer protects the needles from drying out.

96441.q: Does a spruce sometimes lose needles?
a: Yes, single old ones every now and then
Yes, all at once in autumn
96441.e: Evergreen trees renew their needles too. But they only drop single old needles, not all at the same time.
96441.m: Evergreen trees renew their needles bit by bit.

96442.q: Which evergreen shrub is often clipped into balls in the garden?
96442.e: Box has small, dense leaves. That is why it is easy to clip into shape.
96442.m: Box is easy to clip into shape.

96443.q: Which evergreen conifer of the Alps has its needles in bundles of five?
96443.e: The Swiss stone pine grows high in the Alps, for example in the Engadine. Its needles always grow in fives.
96443.m: The Swiss stone pine has needles in fives.

96444.q: How many needles grow together on the Scots pine?
96444.e: On the Scots pine, two long needles always grow together out of a small sheath. That makes it easy to recognise.
96444.m: The Scots pine has needles in pairs.

96445.q: What do deciduous trees do in winter?
96445.e: In winter it is cold and dark. The trees save their strength and wait for spring.

96446.q: What is the time when trees do not grow in winter called?
96446.e: During winter dormancy, trees save their strength. Only when it gets warm again do they carry on growing.

96447.q: How do annual summer flowers survive the winter?
a: As a leaf in the snow
96447.e: Annual plants die in autumn. Only their seeds survive the winter and sprout in spring.
96447.m: Annual plants survive the winter as seeds.

96448.q: What protects small plants on the ground from hard frost?
96448.e: Snow contains a lot of air. That is why it works like a warm blanket for the plants underneath.
96448.m: Snow protects plants like a blanket.

96449.q: In many meadow plants the green parts die in winter. What lives on?
96449.e: The roots in the soil survive the winter. In spring the plant sprouts again from them.
96449.m: In many meadow plants, the roots survive the winter.

96450.q: When do gardeners often prune fruit trees?
a: In high summer in the heat
96450.e: In late winter the tree is resting and has no leaves. That way you can see the branches well and the tree is hardly disturbed.
96450.m: Fruit trees are often pruned in late winter.

96451.q: Where is the best place to keep geraniums over winter?
96451.e: Geraniums cannot cope with frost. In a cool, bright room they rest and can go back outside in spring.
96451.m: Geraniums spend the winter somewhere bright, cool and frost-free.

96452.q: Which cereal is sown in autumn and spends the winter in the field?
96452.e: Winter wheat sprouts in autumn and grows a little. In winter it rests and carries on growing in spring.
96452.m: Winter wheat spends the winter in the field.

96453.q: What happens to hoarfrost when the sun shines warmly?
a: It goes as hard as stone
96453.e: Hoarfrost is frozen water. When it gets warmer, it melts and drips from the branches.
96453.m: Hoarfrost melts in the warm sun.

96454.q: On which side of the branches does hoarfrost grow most?
a: On the side the wind comes from
Only on the side facing the sun
96454.e: The wind blows the tiny fog droplets against the branches. That is why hoarfrost grows towards the wind.
96454.m: Hoarfrost grows on the windward side.

96455.q: Does hoarfrost fall from the sky like snow?
a: No, it grows directly on objects
Yes, but only from clouds at night
96455.e: Hoarfrost does not fall down. It forms directly on branches, fences and grass.
96455.m: Hoarfrost grows on objects and does not fall from the sky.

96456.q: Why can thick hoarfrost make branches break off?
96456.e: When a lot of hoarfrost builds up, it gets heavy. The weight can break thin branches or power lines.

96457.q: In which season do you see hoarfrost?
96457.e: Hoarfrost needs temperatures below zero degrees. Here, that happens mainly in winter.

96458.q: What protects the brain from knocks?
96458.e: The brain lies well protected inside the hard skull. It also floats in a fluid that cushions knocks.

96459.q: How many halves does the cerebrum have?
96459.e: The cerebrum has a left and a right half. A thick band of nerve fibres connects them.

96460.q: What are the cells called that the brain uses to pass on messages?
96460.e: The brain has many billions of nerve cells. They send each other tiny electrical signals.
96460.m: Nerve cells pass on messages in the brain.

96461.q: How do commands get from the brain to the muscles?
96461.e: Nerves run from the brain through the spinal cord to the whole body. The muscles receive their commands through them.
96461.m: Nerves carry the commands to the muscles.

96462.q: What does the surface of the cerebrum look like?
96462.e: The cerebrum is heavily folded, rather like a walnut. That way a large surface fits inside the head.

96463.q: What protects your head and brain when cycling?
96463.e: If you fall, a bike helmet softens the impact. That way it protects the brain from injury.
96463.m: A bike helmet protects the brain.

96464.q: Which half of the brain controls the movements of the right hand?
96464.e: The nerve pathways cross over on their way to the body. That is why the left half of the brain controls the right side of the body.
96464.m: The left half of the brain controls the right hand.

96465.q: Roughly how much of the body's energy does the brain use?
96465.e: The brain is small but uses about 20 percent of the body's energy. So thinking is hard work.
96465.m: The brain uses about a fifth of the energy.

96466.e: With memory the brain stores experiences and knowledge. Later you can remember them.

96467.q: What helps you remember something for a long time?
a: Writing it down quickly and throwing it away
Watching TV at the same time
96467.e: If you practise something again and again, it gets firmly stored in your memory. That way it stays for a long time.
96467.m: If you repeat something often, you remember it for a long time.

96468.q: In which memory does knowledge stay stored for many years?
96468.e: In long-term memory the brain stores knowledge and memories for a very long time. Some things stay for a lifetime.
96468.m: Long-term memory stores knowledge for a long time.

96469.q: What do you call a saying or trick that helps you remember something?
96469.e: A mnemonic links something difficult with something that is easy to remember. Often it is a funny sentence.

96470.q: What does the sentence “My Very Educated Mother Just Served Us Nachos” help you with?
96470.e: The first letters stand for Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. That way you remember the order of the planets.
96470.m: A memory sentence helps with the order of the planets.

96471.q: How can you often remember new things better?
a: By looking at it only once briefly
By listening to loud music at the same time
By watching TV at the same time
96471.e: When you see, hear and try something yourself, the brain lays down several traces. That makes it easier to find the knowledge later.
96471.m: You learn better with several senses.

96472.q: From what age do most people have their first memories?
96472.e: Almost nobody remembers their first years of life. The earliest memories usually come from about the age of 3.
96472.m: First memories usually come from about the age of 3.

96473.q: Which experiences do you usually remember especially well?
96473.e: Strong feelings such as joy or fright show the brain that something is important. That is why it sticks better.
96473.m: Feelings help you remember things better.

96474.q: Roughly how many hours of sleep a night do children aged 6 to 12 need?
96474.e: School-age children need about 9 to 12 hours of sleep. During sleep the body and the brain recover.
96474.m: Schoolchildren need 9 to 12 hours of sleep.

96475.q: What moves quickly back and forth during the dreaming phase of sleep?
96475.e: In the dreaming phase the eyes move quickly under the closed lids. In this phase dreams are especially vivid.
96475.m: In the dreaming phase the eyes move quickly.

96476.q: What does the brain do during sleep with what you have learnt?
96476.e: During sleep the brain goes over what you have learnt and stores it more firmly. That is why good sleep helps you learn.
96476.m: During sleep the brain stores what you have learnt.

96477.q: What do you call a bad, scary dream?
96477.e: A nightmare is frightening, and sometimes you wake up from it. Nightmares are common in children and pass.
96477.m: A nightmare is a scary dream.

96478.q: What is it called when someone walks around in their sleep?
96478.e: When sleepwalking, someone gets up in deep sleep and walks around. In the morning they usually know nothing about it.
96478.m: Someone who walks around in their sleep is sleepwalking.

96479.q: What often makes it harder to fall asleep?
a: Bright screen light just before bed
96479.e: The bright light of phones and tablets wakes the brain up. So it is better to put screens away early in the evening.
96479.m: Screen light in the evening makes it harder to fall asleep.

96480.q: Roughly how many hours a day does a newborn baby sleep?
96480.e: Newborns sleep for most of the day. But they wake up often because they are hungry.

96481.q: Do you dream even on nights when you don't remember any dream?
96481.e: Almost everyone dreams several times every night. But often you have already forgotten the dreams when you wake up.
96481.m: You dream even if you don't remember it in the morning.

96482.q: What does it mean to pay attention?
96482.e: If you pay attention, you focus your thoughts on one thing. You notice other things less.

96483.q: What disturbs your concentration most when doing homework?
96483.e: Every beep pulls your attention away. Afterwards the brain needs time to get back to the task.

96484.q: What helps when you can't concentrate well any more?
a: A short break with some movement
96484.e: After a while the brain gets tired. A short break in the fresh air helps you pay attention again.

96485.q: What usually happens when you do two tasks at the same time?
96485.e: The brain is bad at concentrating on two things at once. It jumps back and forth and makes mistakes.
96485.m: Doing two things at once leads to more mistakes.

96486.q: Why shouldn't you look at your phone when crossing the road?
96486.e: If you look at your phone, you don't watch the traffic. It is easy to miss a car or a bike.
96486.m: In traffic, your attention belongs on the road.

96487.q: In a famous experiment, people count passes of a ball in a film. What do many of them miss?
a: A person in a gorilla costume
96487.e: Many viewers concentrate so hard on counting that they don't see the gorilla at all. This shows how selective attention is.
96487.m: If you concentrate hard, you miss other things.

96488.q: What do you often still hear straight away in a loud room full of voices?
a: A quiet whisper in the next room
96488.e: Even in noise the brain listens out for important words. Your own name is one of them.
96488.m: You hear your own name even in noise.

96489.q: What helps the brain stay alert?
a: Studying without breakfast and drinking nothing
96489.e: Even being a little thirsty can make concentration worse. So it is best to have a glass of water ready while you study.
96489.m: Drinking water helps you pay attention.

a: A picture you see differently from how it really is
A picture you can only see in the dark
96490.e: With an optical illusion, a picture looks different from how it really is. For example, lines of the same length seem to be different lengths.
96490.m: With an optical illusion you see something differently from how it is.

96491.q: Who is actually being tricked by an optical illusion?
96491.e: The eyes take in the picture correctly. It is the brain that interprets it wrongly.
96491.m: With optical illusions the brain gets it wrong.

96492.q: How do two lines of the same length look if one has arrowheads pointing inwards and the other outwards?
96492.e: This illusion is called the Müller-Lyer illusion. Although both lines are the same length, one looks longer.
96492.m: Arrowheads make equal lines look different lengths.

96493.q: Where does the full moon look bigger, even though it stays the same size?
96493.e: When the moon is low over houses or mountains, the brain judges it to be bigger. This is called the moon illusion.
96493.m: The moon looks bigger near the horizon.

96494.q: Why do you see movement in a flip book?
a: The pictures follow each other very quickly
The pictures move on the paper
96494.e: When many slightly different pictures come quickly one after another, the brain joins them into movement. A film works the same way.
96494.m: Quick sequences of pictures look like movement.

96495.q: What do you call a picture in which you see two things in turn, for example a rabbit or a duck?
