96495.e: With an ambiguous image the brain jumps back and forth between two interpretations. You can hardly see both at once.
96495.m: An ambiguous image shows two things in one picture.

96496.q: What does a straight drinking straw look like in a glass of water?
96496.e: Light is bent as it passes from water into air. That is why the straw seems to have a kink at the surface of the water.
96496.m: A straw in water looks bent.

96497.q: What do you call a mirage in the desert that looks like a lake?
96497.e: Hot air above the ground bends the light. You see the sky reflected, and it looks like water.
96497.m: A Fata Morgana looks like water in the desert.

96498.e: A reflex happens automatically; you don't have to plan it. Many reflexes protect the body.

96499.q: What happens when the doctor taps just below the kneecap with a little hammer?
96499.e: This is the knee-jerk reflex. The doctor uses it to check whether the nerves are working well.
96499.m: When tapped below the knee, the leg jerks forward.

96500.q: What does your hand do when it touches a hot hob?
96500.e: The hand jerks back before you really feel the pain. This reflex protects against bad burns.
96500.m: With heat, you pull your hand back in a flash.

96501.q: What do your eyes do when something suddenly flies towards them?
96501.e: The blink reflex protects the eyes. The lids shut before you even think about it.
96501.m: When there is danger, your eyes close by themselves.

96502.q: Which reflex clears your nose when it tickles?
96502.e: When you sneeze, air shoots through your nose with great force. Dust and crumbs are blown out.

96503.q: What does the body do when food goes down the wrong way?
96503.e: The cough reflex throws food or mucus out of the airways. Then you can breathe properly again.

96504.q: What does a baby do when you put a finger in its hand?
96504.e: Newborns have a grasp reflex. It disappears again after a few months.

96505.q: What do the pupils do when bright light shines into the eye?
96505.e: In bright light the pupils contract. That way less light gets into the eye.
96505.m: In bright light the pupils get small.

96506.q: How many senses are usually listed at school?
96506.e: People usually name sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch. There are also other senses besides these.

96507.q: Which sense organ do you smell with?
96507.e: There are smell cells in the nose. They recognise thousands of different smells.

96508.q: Which sense organ do you taste with?
96508.e: There are many taste buds on the tongue. With them you can taste things like sweet and sour.

96509.q: What is the largest sense organ of the human body?
96509.e: The skin covers the whole body. With it you feel touch, warmth, cold and pain.
96509.m: The skin is the largest sense organ.

96510.q: Which of these is a basic taste of the tongue?
96510.e: The basic tastes are sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami. Spicy heat is actually a mild pain.

96511.q: Why does food often taste bland when you have a cold?
96511.e: A large part of taste actually comes from the nose. If it is blocked, lots of things taste the same.

96512.q: Which sense does a blind person use to read braille?
96512.e: Braille is made of raised dots. You read it with your fingertips.
96512.m: Braille is read with the sense of touch.

96513.q: Which pet can smell much better than a human?
96513.e: Dogs have many more smell cells than humans. That is why they can sniff out trails and search for missing people.
96513.m: Dogs smell much better than humans.

96514.q: Which sense tells you what colour an apple is?
96514.e: You see colours with your eyes. The eye has cells that tell red, green and blue apart.
96514.m: You recognise colours with your sense of sight.

96515.q: Where is the organ of balance?
96515.e: The organ of balance lies deep in the ear, right next to the hearing organ. It tells the brain about every turn and tilt.
96515.m: The organ of balance is in the inner ear.

96516.q: How do you feel when you have spun round quickly for a long time and then stop?
96516.e: After spinning, the organ of balance is confused. That is why everything seems to keep turning.

96517.q: Why does everything keep spinning after a merry-go-round ride?
a: The fluid in the inner ear keeps moving
The merry-go-round keeps turning in your head
96517.e: Fluid sloshes about in the organ of balance. After stopping, it keeps turning for a moment and tricks the brain.
96517.m: The fluid in the ear keeps turning.

96518.q: Why is it harder to stand on one leg with your eyes closed?
a: Your ears can't hear anything then
96518.e: The brain also uses the eyes for balance. Without this help you wobble more.

96519.q: What is the sickness called that some people get when reading in a moving car?
96519.e: The organ of balance feels the movement, but the eyes see a still book. This confusion can make you feel sick.
96519.m: Reading in the car can cause travel sickness.

96520.q: What do you mainly train when balancing on a slackline?
96520.e: On the narrow, wobbly strap you constantly have to adjust. That trains your sense of balance.
96520.m: On a slackline you train your balance.

96521.q: Which animal usually twists while falling so that it lands on its paws?
96521.e: When falling, a cat senses exactly where up and down are. It turns in a flash and usually lands on its paws.
96521.m: Cats usually land on their paws.

96522.q: How many semicircular canals does the organ of balance have in each ear?
96522.e: Each organ of balance has three semicircular canals. They point in different directions and report turns.
96522.m: The organ of balance has three semicircular canals.

a: Someone who is more skilful with their left hand
Someone who only sees to the left
Someone who lives on the left
Someone who sleeps on the left
96523.e: Left-handers usually write, draw and throw with their left hand. For them, that hand is more skilful.
96523.m: Left-handers are more skilful with their left hand.

96524.q: What do experts advise for a left-handed child?
a: Let them write with their left hand
Force them to write with their right
Not let them write at all
96524.e: In the past, left-handers were often forced to write with their right hand. Today we know that this can be harmful.
96524.m: Left-handers should be allowed to write with their left hand.

96525.q: Which tool is there at school especially for left-handers?
96525.e: On left-handed scissors the blades are swapped round. That way a left-hander can see the line while cutting.
96525.m: There are special scissors for left-handers.

96526.q: There are 20 children in a class. Roughly how many of them are left-handed?
96526.e: About one in ten children is left-handed. In a class of 20 children, that is about 2.
96526.m: About one child in ten is left-handed.

96527.q: What do you call people who can use both hands equally well?
96527.e: Truly ambidextrous people are rare. They can write or throw almost equally well with their left and right hand.
96527.m: Ambidextrous people are equally skilful with both hands.

96528.q: Why do left-handers sometimes smudge what they have written in ink?
a: Their hand moves over the fresh writing
96528.e: We write from left to right. A left-hander pushes their hand over what they have just written.
96528.m: Left-handers move their hand over the fresh writing.

96529.q: Are there also people who are more skilful with their left foot?
96529.e: Just as with hands, there is also a preferred foot. In football, left-footed players prefer to shoot with their left.
96529.m: Left-footed players prefer to shoot with their left.

96530.q: What helps most when learning to play an instrument well?
96530.e: With regular practice the movements become more and more confident. In time, playing works almost by itself.

96531.q: What usually works better when learning?
a: Practising for a very long time once a month
Only studying the day before the test
96531.e: Short practice sessions on many days fix knowledge better. In between, the brain has time to sort everything out.
96531.m: Practising a little every day works best.

96532.q: What happens in your head when you practise something often?
a: You remember it better and better
It makes you tired and you never manage it
96532.e: When you practise, the brain uses the same paths again and again. They get stronger, like a trodden path through grass.
96532.m: Practice strengthens the paths in the brain.

96533.q: What are mistakes good for when practising?
a: They show that you should stop
96533.e: A mistake shows what you can still improve. If you notice it and correct it, you learn something.

96534.q: What do you hardly ever forget if you practised it well as a child?
a: The name of a random street
96534.e: The brain stores movements you have practised often for a very long time. That is why you can still ride a bike after many years.
96534.m: You hardly ever forget how to ride a bike.

96535.q: How does the saying “Practice makes ...” continue?
96535.e: The saying “Practice makes perfect” means that you get good by practising. Nobody can do everything right from the start.

96536.q: What helps especially well when practising for a test?
a: Just putting the exercise book under your pillow
96536.e: If you test yourself, you have to actively pull the knowledge out of your memory. That way it sticks better.

96537.q: What do you need when practising if something doesn't work straight away?
96537.e: Many things take lots of attempts. With patience and perseverance you get better step by step.

96538.q: When do you forget most of something you have just learnt?
96538.e: New things are lost fastest in the first hours and days. This is shown by the so-called forgetting curve.
96538.m: You forget most shortly after learning.

a: Going over what you have learnt
Not thinking about it at all
96539.e: Each time you go over it, the memory gets stronger. It is best to revise after one day, then again after a few days.

a: The brain gets rid of unimportant things
You never have to learn again
96540.e: The brain cannot keep every little detail. Forgetting leaves room for what is important.

96541.q: What do you say when you can almost think of a word, but not quite?
a: It's on the tip of my tongue
96541.e: You know that you know the word, but you just can't find it. Often it comes to you a little later.
96541.m: When a word almost comes to you, it's on the tip of your tongue.

96542.q: What did people do in the past to remind themselves of something?
a: Tie a knot in a handkerchief
Put a stone in their shoe
Wear their hat back to front
Put a spoon in their pocket
96542.e: They would notice the knot in the handkerchief later. Then they knew they had to remember something.
96542.m: A knot in a handkerchief used to be a memory aid.

96543.q: What helps you not to forget anything when shopping?
96543.e: A shopping list has everything you need on it. That way you don't have to remember it.
96543.m: A shopping list helps against forgetting.

96544.q: What happens if you don't get enough sleep?
96544.e: Without enough sleep the brain is worse at storing what you have learnt. You become more forgetful and less focused.
96544.m: If you sleep too little, you forget more.

96545.q: How are you least likely to forget where your house key is?
a: You always put it in the same place
You put it somewhere different every day
You hide it in the garden
You throw it in a drawer full of stuff
96545.e: What you always do the same way becomes a habit. Then you don't have to remember the place each time.
96545.m: A fixed place helps you not to forget things.

96547.e: 15 minus 5 makes 10, then take away 1 more makes 9.

96548.e: 6 times 8 makes 48. So 48 divided by 6 is 8.

96550.q: What is an easy way to add 9 in your head?
96550.e: 9 is 1 less than 10. So you add 10 and then take 1 away again.
96550.m: To add 9, add 10 and take away 1.

96551.e: Double 30 is 60, double 5 is 10. Together that makes 70.

96552.e: Half of 80 is 40, half of 10 is 5. Together that makes 45.

96553.q: A piece of chewing gum costs 50 centimes. How much do 4 pieces cost?
96553.e: 4 times 50 centimes makes 200 centimes. 100 centimes are 1 franc, so that is 2 francs.

96554.e: 100 minus 30 makes 70. Then take away 7 more makes 63.

96555.q: In which organ do we store our memories?
96555.e: Memory is in the brain. Experiences and knowledge are stored there.
96555.m: Our memories are stored in the brain.

96556.q: What helps your memory hold on to what you have learnt?
96556.e: During sleep, the brain sorts out what we learnt during the day. That way it sticks better.
96556.m: If you sleep well, you remember what you learn better.

96557.q: What is the memory that only remembers things for a short time called?
96557.e: Short-term memory only holds a few things for a short time. After that, much is forgotten again.
96557.m: Short-term memory only remembers things for a short time.

96558.q: Where do memories stay stored for many years?
96558.e: Long-term memory can store knowledge and experiences for a whole lifetime.
96558.m: Long-term memory stores things for a long time.

96559.q: How can you remember a long phone number more easily?
96559.e: The brain can remember small groups of numbers much more easily than one long row.
96559.m: Long numbers are easier to remember in small groups.

96560.e: A mnemonic is a trick that helps you remember something better, for example a short rhyme.

96561.q: Which animal is said never to forget anything?
96561.e: People say someone has a memory like an elephant. Elephants really can remember paths and other elephants for many years.
96561.m: Elephants are known for their good memory.

96562.q: What is it called when you no longer know something?
96562.e: When you can no longer recall a memory, you have forgotten it. That is completely normal.

96563.q: Which time of their life can adults usually not remember?
96563.e: Memories of the first two to three years of life are almost always lost. At that time the brain is still growing a lot.
96563.m: Later on, you hardly remember your first years of life.

96564.q: What happens to many dreams shortly after waking up?
a: You carry on dreaming them at once
96564.e: Most dreams are forgotten after a few minutes. If you want to keep them, write them down straight away.
96564.m: You forget many dreams shortly after waking up.

96565.q: What do you call a dream that frightens you?
96565.e: A nightmare is an unpleasant dream that you often wake up from with a start.
96565.m: A nightmare is a dream that frightens you.

96566.e: Everyone dreams every night, even if they often cannot remember it in the morning.
96566.m: Everyone dreams, even if they forget it.

96567.q: What is it called when you are awake and dream with your eyes open?
96567.e: When daydreaming, your thoughts wander even though you are awake. You often imagine nice things.
96567.m: You have daydreams while you are awake.

96568.q: In which animal can you often see signs of dreaming during sleep, such as twitching paws?
96568.e: Like people, dogs have a dreaming phase in their sleep. Their paws sometimes twitch or they bark quietly.
96568.m: Dogs also have a dreaming phase in their sleep.

96569.q: What is a dream in which you realise that you are dreaming called?
96569.e: In a lucid dream you know that you are dreaming. Some people can even steer their dream then.
96569.m: In a lucid dream you know you are dreaming.

96570.q: Where does the dreamcatcher originally come from?
96570.e: Dreamcatchers come from the Native peoples of North America. According to their belief, they keep bad dreams away.
96570.m: The dreamcatcher comes from the Native peoples of North America.

96571.q: What happens in the brain when we learn something?
96571.e: When we learn, nerve cells make new connections. The more often you practise, the stronger they get.
96571.m: Learning makes new connections in the brain.

96572.e: What you repeat often stays much better in your memory. Practice makes perfect.

96573.q: How do babies learn to speak?
96573.e: Babies listen to the people around them and copy the sounds. That way they learn words little by little.
96573.m: Babies learn to speak by listening and copying.

96574.q: At what age do children in Switzerland usually start kindergarten?
96574.e: In most cantons, kindergarten starts at about four years old. It usually lasts two years.
96574.m: In Switzerland, kindergarten usually starts at about four.

96575.q: Why are short breaks important when learning?
96575.e: In short breaks, the brain recovers. Afterwards you can pay attention better again.
96575.m: Short breaks give the brain new energy.

96576.q: What are cards with the question on the front and the answer on the back called?
96576.e: With flashcards you can test yourself. They help, for example, when learning new words.
96576.m: With flashcards you can test yourself.

96577.q: What is completely normal when learning and even helps you along?
96577.e: From mistakes you notice what you still need to practise. That way you learn more.
96577.m: You can learn a lot from mistakes.

96578.q: What is the best way to learn to ride a bike?
96578.e: You only learn to ride a bike by trying it yourself again and again. The body has to practise balancing.
96578.m: You learn to ride a bike by practising.

a: To keep your attention on one thing
To run as fast as possible
96579.e: When you concentrate, you put all your attention on one task.
96579.m: Concentrating means sticking with one thing.

96580.q: What disturbs your concentration when doing homework?
96580.e: Noise distracts you because the brain keeps listening. A quiet place helps you work.

96581.q: What helps your head stay focused?
96581.e: The brain needs enough fluid. Water is the best drink for this.
96581.m: Drinking water helps your head think.

96582.q: What helps you pay attention again after sitting for a long time?
a: Putting your head on the desk
96582.e: Movement gets your circulation going. Afterwards you can concentrate better again.

96583.q: Which mid-morning snack gives your head good energy?
a: An apple and a piece of bread
96583.e: Fruit and bread give energy for a long time. Lots of sugar only gives a short boost.
96583.m: A healthy mid-morning snack gives your head long-lasting energy.

96584.q: What usually happens when you do two tasks at the same time?
96584.e: The brain is bad at concentrating on two things at once. That is why more mistakes happen.
96584.m: One task after another works better.

96585.q: Which device often distracts you when learning?
96585.e: Messages and games on the phone pull your attention away. That is why it is better to put it away while learning.
96585.m: When learning, it is better to put your phone away.

96586.q: Which simple exercise helps you become calm and attentive?
96586.e: Calm, deep breathing relaxes the body. Afterwards it is easier to concentrate.

96587.e: Curious people want to find out how things work. Curiosity drives learning.
96587.m: Curious people want to know new things.

96588.q: Which question word do curious children use especially often?
96588.e: With “Why?” children ask for reasons. Small children ask lots and lots of why questions.
96588.m: With “Why?” you ask for the reason.

96589.q: Which animal is seen as especially curious in many stories?
96589.e: Cats like to explore every corner. That is why there is an English saying that curiosity killed the cat.
96589.m: Cats are seen as very curious.

96590.q: What is the curious little monkey from children's books and cartoons called?
96590.e: Curious George, called Coco in German, is a curious monkey. His curiosity keeps leading him into funny adventures.
96590.m: Curious George is a curious little monkey.

96591.q: How does curiosity help with learning?
a: You want to find out more
96591.e: If you are curious, you want to understand things and you ask questions. That way you learn all by yourself.

96592.q: A robot rover on Mars is called “Curiosity”. What does that word mean?
96592.e: Curiosity means wanting to know and find out things. The rover has been exploring Mars since 2012.
96592.m: Curiosity means wanting to find things out.

96593.q: What do you call people who are curious and find out new things?
96593.e: Researchers ask questions and look for answers with experiments.
96593.m: Researchers look for answers to new questions.

a: Making things up in your head
96594.e: With your imagination you picture things that do not exist or that you cannot see.
96594.m: With imagination you make things up.

96595.q: Which animal only exists in the imagination?
96595.e: The unicorn is a mythical creature from legends and fairy tales. In reality there is no unicorn.
96595.m: The unicorn is a mythical creature.

96596.q: According to legend, on which mountain near Lucerne did dragons live?
96596.e: Many legends tell of dragons on Pilatus. That is why the dragon is a symbol of the mountain today.
96596.m: According to legend, dragons lived on Pilatus.

96597.q: For what do you need especially much imagination?
96597.e: When you make up a story, you invent characters, places and adventures.
96597.m: To make up stories you need imagination.

96598.q: What is a made-up story with witches, fairies and magic called?
96598.e: Fairy tales are made-up stories, often with magic. The fairy tales of the Brothers Grimm are well known.
96598.m: Fairy tales are made-up stories full of magic.

96599.q: What do you call a friend that a child only imagines?
96599.e: Many children have an imaginary friend for a while. That is completely normal and shows a lot of imagination.
96599.m: An imaginary friend only exists in the imagination.

96600.q: Which mythical creature is half human and half fish?
96600.e: The mermaid has a human body and a fish tail. She appears in many fairy tales.
96600.m: The mermaid is half human and half fish.

96601.q: What is a game in which you pretend to be someone else called?
96601.e: In role play you play a doctor, a pirate or a queen, for example. You need lots of imagination for it.
96601.m: In role play you take on a different role.

96603.q: What often helps with a mild headache?
a: Sitting at a screen for a long time
96603.e: A mild headache often comes from too little fluid or tiredness. Drinking and rest then often help.
96603.m: With a mild headache, drinking and rest often help.

96604.q: What can cause a short stabbing pain in the head?
a: Eating very cold ice cream quickly
96604.e: When something very cold touches the roof of the mouth, blood vessels react. This gives a short, stabbing headache.
96604.m: Ice cream eaten too quickly can give you a short headache.

96605.q: Which part of the head cannot feel pain itself?
96605.e: The brain has no pain sensors of its own. Headaches come from places like the membranes around the brain, blood vessels or muscles.
96605.m: The brain itself feels no pain.

a: Looking at a screen for too long
96606.e: Staring at screens for a long time strains your eyes and neck. That can cause a headache.
96606.m: Too much screen time can cause headaches.

96607.q: What are strong headaches called that keep coming back and often affect only one side?
96607.e: Migraine is a special kind of headache. Bright light or noise is often bothersome then too.
96607.m: Migraine is a strong headache that keeps coming back.

96608.q: What should you do if a headache is very bad or does not go away for a long time?
96608.e: With a very bad or long-lasting headache, a doctor should take a look.
96608.m: A doctor should look at a bad headache.

96609.q: What can feel nice when you have a headache?
a: A cool cloth on the forehead
96609.e: Many people find coolness on the forehead soothing when they have a headache.
96609.m: A cool cloth can help with a headache.

96610.q: What can cause a headache when you sit hunched for a long time?
96610.e: Sitting hunched makes the neck muscles tense. That can lead to a headache.
96610.m: Sitting up straight is good for your neck and head.

96611.q: How much space should there be between your chin and the chin strap of your bike helmet?
96611.e: The strap should fit snugly but not press. One finger should still fit in between.
96611.m: One finger fits between chin and strap.

96612.q: What should you do with your bike helmet after a bad fall?
96612.e: After a hard impact, the helmet can be damaged inside even if you cannot see anything. That is why you need a new helmet.
96612.m: After a fall you need a new helmet.

96613.q: For which vehicle is a helmet compulsory in Switzerland?
96613.e: On fast e-bikes that assist up to 45 km/h, a helmet is compulsory in Switzerland. On a normal bike it is strongly recommended.
96613.m: On fast e-bikes, a helmet is compulsory.

96614.q: When should you wear a bike helmet?
96614.e: Accidents can happen even on short journeys. That is why the helmet goes on your head for every ride.
96614.m: The bike helmet goes on your head for every ride.

96615.q: What does the foam in a bike helmet do in a fall?
96615.e: The hard foam absorbs the force of the impact. That way the head is hit less hard.
96615.m: The foam in the helmet cushions the impact.

96616.q: Which colour makes a bike helmet easy to see in traffic?
96616.e: Drivers see light and bright colours sooner. That makes cycling safer.
96616.m: Bright colours make you easier to see.

96617.q: Where is a bike helmet fastened with a strap?
96617.e: The chin strap holds the helmet in place. Only a fastened helmet can protect you properly.
96617.m: The helmet is fastened under the chin.

96618.q: What do nerves carry through the body?
96618.e: Nerves carry signals back and forth between the brain and the body, a bit like cables.

96619.q: What is the thick bundle of nerves in the back called?
96619.e: The spinal cord connects the brain with the nerves in the whole body. It lies protected inside the spine.
96619.m: The spinal cord connects the brain and the body.

96620.q: Which bones protect the spinal cord?
96620.e: The spinal cord runs through a channel in the vertebrae of the spine. That way it is well protected.
96620.m: The vertebrae protect the spinal cord.

96621.q: What does “That gets on my nerves” mean?
96621.e: The saying means that something annoys or bothers you.
96621.m: Something that gets on your nerves bothers you.

96622.q: What are the cells that make up the brain and nerves called?
96622.e: Nerve cells can receive signals and pass them on. Experts also call them neurons.
96622.m: The brain and nerves are made of nerve cells.

96623.q: Why does it tingle so much when you knock your elbow?
a: A nerve lies close under the skin there
There is a big muscle there
There is a rubber joint there
96623.e: At the so-called funny bone, a nerve lies very close under the skin. A knock irritates it directly.
96623.m: At the funny bone, a nerve lies right under the skin.

96624.q: What do nerves in the skin report to the brain?
a: Whether something is hot or cold
96624.e: In the skin there are nerve endings for warmth, cold, pressure and pain.
96624.m: Nerves in the skin feel warmth and cold.

96625.q: Why does a leg sometimes “go to sleep”?
96625.e: If you sit on a leg for a long time, nerves get squashed. For a while they do not pass on signals well, and it tingles.
96625.m: A leg that has gone to sleep comes from a squashed nerve.

96626.q: Roughly how many nerve cells does the brain have?
96626.e: Scientists estimate that the human brain has around 86 billion nerve cells.
96626.m: The brain has about 86 billion nerve cells.

96627.q: What do you do by reflex when you touch a hot hob?
96627.e: The body pulls the hand back in a flash, even before you really feel the pain.
96627.m: When something is hot, you pull your hand back in a flash.

96628.q: What do your eyes do when something suddenly flies towards them?
96628.e: The blink reflex closes the eyes very quickly. That way they are protected.
96628.m: The eyes close by themselves for protection.

96629.q: What does the doctor use to test a reflex at the knee?
96629.e: If you tap just below the kneecap, the lower leg jerks forwards. That is the knee reflex.
96629.m: A small hammer is used to test the knee reflex.

96630.q: When do you react more slowly?
96630.e: Tiredness makes the brain slower. That is why you then take longer to react.

96631.q: Can a fast car stop immediately when it brakes hard?
a: No, it needs a stopping distance
Yes, even faster in the rain
96631.e: The driver needs time to react, and the car keeps rolling a bit further while braking. That is why children learn: wait, look, listen, walk.
96631.m: A car needs time and distance to stop.

96632.q: Roughly how long does a fast reaction to a signal take?
96632.e: People usually react to a simple signal in about a fifth of a second.
96632.m: A fast reaction takes less than a second.

96633.q: How can you test your reactions with a ruler?
a: Drop it and catch it quickly
96633.e: Someone lets go of the ruler and you catch it as quickly as possible. The shorter the distance it falls, the faster your reaction.
96633.m: You can measure your reactions with a falling ruler.

a: A dance in the sports hall
96634.e: In brain training you exercise your thinking, for example with puzzles and thinking games.
96634.m: Brain training is exercise for your head.

96635.q: What is the number puzzle with 9 by 9 squares called?
96635.e: In sudoku you fill a grid of 81 squares with numbers so that no number is repeated in a row, column or box.
96635.m: Sudoku is a number puzzle with 81 squares.

96636.q: Which numbers do you write into a normal sudoku?
96636.e: The numbers 1 to 9 go into every row, every column and every box exactly once.
96636.m: A sudoku contains the numbers 1 to 9.

96637.q: Which board game with a king and queen trains your thinking especially well?
96637.e: In chess you have to plan your moves ahead. In snakes and ladders and bingo, luck mostly decides.
96637.m: Chess trains you to think ahead.

96638.q: In which puzzle do you write words into squares that cross each other?
96638.e: In a crossword the words cross. One letter then belongs to two words.
96638.m: In a crossword, words cross each other.

96639.e: The sequence counts in fives. After 15 comes 15 plus 5, which is 20.
96639.m: In the five times table, 20 comes after 15.

96640.q: Which name reads exactly the same backwards?
96640.e: Anna read backwards is Anna again. Words like this are called palindromes.
96640.m: A palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards.

96641.q: Which is heavier: a kilo of feathers or a kilo of stones?
96641.e: A kilo is always a kilo. The feathers just take up much more space.
96641.m: A kilo always weighs the same.

a: When you do not know what to do
96642.e: You feel bored when nothing exciting is happening and you have nothing to do.
96642.m: You are bored when nothing exciting is happening.

96643.q: What can you do about boredom?
96643.e: A book, a game or a craft brings new thoughts. Then the boredom goes away.
96643.m: An exciting activity helps against boredom.

96644.e: When your head has nothing to do, your thoughts wander. New ideas often come up that way.
96644.m: New ideas often come from boredom.

96645.q: What does the body often do when you are bored?
96645.e: Many people yawn when they are bored or tired.
96645.m: You often yawn when you are bored.

96647.e: L'ennui means boredom. La joie is joy, la peur is fear and la faim is hunger.

96648.q: How does time feel when you are bored?
96648.e: When you are bored, you pay close attention to time. That is why it seems especially long.
96648.m: When you are bored, time seems to pass slowly.

96649.q: Which game can you play on a long car journey without any equipment?
96649.e: In this guessing game, you describe something you can see and the others guess. You only need your eyes.
96649.m: Guessing games help against boredom on long journeys.

96650.q: Apart from between a cloud and the ground, where else can lightning jump?
a: Between two houses in the cellar
96650.e: Most lightning doesn't strike the ground at all. It jumps back and forth inside a cloud or between clouds.
96650.m: Lots of lightning stays in the clouds.

96651.q: How long does a flash of lightning usually last?
96651.e: Lightning flashes incredibly fast. It is usually over in a fraction of a second.
96651.m: A flash of lightning usually lasts less than a second.

96652.q: About how hot does the air in a lightning bolt get?
96652.e: Lightning heats the air up to about 30,000 degrees Celsius. That is hotter than the surface of the Sun.
96652.m: Lightning is hotter than the surface of the Sun.

96653.q: About how often is there lightning around the whole world?
96653.e: Across the whole Earth, about 40 to 50 flashes of lightning happen every second.
96653.m: There is lightning on Earth many times every second.

96654.q: What shape does lightning usually have in the sky?
96654.e: Lightning finds its way through the air in lots of small pieces. That is why it looks jagged and branched.

96655.q: In which canton does lightning strike most often in Switzerland?
96655.e: In Ticino there are especially many thunderstorms in summer. That is usually where the most lightning strikes in Switzerland are counted.
96655.m: In Switzerland, there is most lightning in Ticino.

96656.q: What is the flickering light of a faraway thunderstorm, when you can't hear any thunder, called?
96656.e: With heat lightning, the storm is so far away that the thunder no longer reaches us. You only see the light on the horizon.
96656.m: Heat lightning is the light of a distant thunderstorm.

96657.q: Can lightning strike the same place twice?
96657.e: Tall buildings such as towers are actually hit very often. The saying that lightning never strikes twice is not true.
96657.m: Lightning can strike the same place several times.

96658.q: What should you do in a thunderstorm if you can't find shelter outdoors?
a: Crouch down with your feet together
96658.e: Crouching with your feet together makes you small. Lying flat is more dangerous because the current can flow through the ground.
96658.m: Without shelter, crouch down with your feet together.

96659.q: In which season are there the most thunderstorms in Switzerland?
96659.e: In summer it is warm and humid. Then warm air rises and forms tall thunderclouds.

96660.q: Where are you safest in a thunderstorm?
96660.e: A house protects you from lightning. Single trees, summits and water are dangerous in a thunderstorm.
96660.m: In a thunderstorm, it is best to go indoors.

96661.q: What should you do in a thunderstorm at the swimming pool or lake?
a: Get out of the water immediately
96661.e: Water conducts electricity, and in shallow water you are often the highest point. That is why you must get out straight away.
96661.m: In a thunderstorm, get out of the water immediately.

96662.q: Why are you fairly safe in a car during a thunderstorm?
a: The metal body carries the current round the outside
The tyres are made of rubber
96662.e: The metal body of the car carries the lightning current round the outside of the people and into the ground.
96662.m: The metal body of a car protects you from lightning.

96663.q: What do clouds look like when a thunderstorm is coming soon?
a: Flat and light grey like fog
96663.e: Thunderclouds tower many kilometres high and become very dark at the bottom. At the top they often look like an anvil.
96663.m: Thunderstorms come from tall, dark clouds.

96664.q: What sometimes falls from the sky as balls of ice in strong summer thunderstorms?
96664.e: In tall thunderclouds, water drops freeze into balls of ice. They fall down as hail.
96664.m: Hailstones are balls of ice from thunderclouds.

96665.q: How can you estimate how far away a thunderstorm is?
a: Count the seconds between lightning and thunder
96665.e: Light is much faster than sound. The more seconds pass between lightning and thunder, the further away the storm is. About three seconds means roughly one kilometre.
96665.m: If you count the seconds until the thunder, you know how far away the storm is.

96666.q: What does the Greek word “elektron”, which “electricity” comes from, mean?
96666.e: The ancient Greeks already noticed that rubbed amber attracts small things. The Greek word for amber is elektron.
96666.m: The word electricity comes from the Greek word for amber.

96667.q: What are the two kinds of electric charge?
96667.e: Electric charges are either positive, that is plus, or negative, that is minus.
96667.m: There are positive and negative charges.

96668.q: What do two like charges, for example plus and plus, do?
96668.e: Like charges repel each other. This is true for plus and plus, and also for minus and minus.

96669.q: What do plus and minus do to each other?
96669.e: Opposite charges attract each other, a bit like the north and south poles of magnets.
96669.m: Plus and minus attract each other.

96670.q: What are the tiny particles that move from one thing to another when you rub them called?
96670.e: When you rub things, electrons jump from one material to the other. So one object becomes negatively charged and the other positively.
96670.m: When you rub things, electrons move.

96671.e: Electrons are always negatively charged. Anything that gains electrons becomes negative.

96672.q: What is different about electricity from rubbing compared with electricity from a socket?
96672.e: With rubbing, charge collects on an object and stays there. That is why it is called resting or static electricity.
96672.m: Static electricity is charge that stays still.

96673.q: What did the ancient Greeks already notice when they rubbed amber with wool?
a: It attracted light things like feathers
It began to glow in the dark
96673.e: Rubbed amber becomes electrically charged and attracts light things. The Greek word for amber is “elektron”, which is where the word electricity comes from.
96673.m: The word electricity comes from the Greek word for amber.

96674.q: When do you get charged with static electricity especially easily?
a: When the air is dry in winter
When the air is humid in summer
96674.e: Dry air is bad at carrying charge away. That is why there is more crackling and sparking in heated rooms in winter.
96674.m: You get charged more easily when the air is dry.

96675.q: What can happen when you slide down a plastic slide?
96675.e: Your clothes rub against the plastic as you slide. This charges up your body.
96675.m: Sliding on plastic charges you up.

96676.q: What happens to your hair when it is strongly charged with electricity?
96676.e: All the hairs then have the same charge and repel each other. That is why they stand on end.

96677.q: On which kind of floor do you often get charged up as you walk?
96677.e: When you shuffle across a carpet, your soles rub against it. This charges up your body.
96677.m: You easily get charged up on carpets.

96678.q: Why do socks sometimes stick together when they come out of the tumble dryer?
a: They are sticky from the washing powder
96678.e: In the tumble dryer, the clothes rub against each other for a long time. They get charged and then attract each other.
96678.m: Washing from the tumble dryer is often electrically charged.

96679.q: What helps against getting a shock from the door handle?
a: Touching the door handle with a key first
Shuffling across the carpet in socks
96679.e: The key carries the charge away, and the spark jumps at the key instead of at your finger.
96679.m: A key can gently carry the charge away.

96681.q: Where does the electric eel live?
96681.e: The electric eel lives in rivers and swamps in South America, for example in the Amazon region.
96681.m: The electric eel lives in South America.

96682.q: How long can an electric eel grow?
96682.e: Large electric eels grow up to about 2.5 metres long. Most of their body is made up of the organs that produce electricity.
96682.m: An electric eel can grow over two metres long.

96683.q: What does the electric eel use its strong electric shocks for?
96683.e: With strong shocks it stuns prey fish and fights off enemies.
96683.m: The electric eel hunts with electricity.

96684.q: Is the electric eel really an eel?
96684.e: The electric eel looks like an eel, but it belongs to the American knifefishes.
96684.m: The electric eel is not really an eel.

96685.q: What kind of water does the electric eel live in?
96685.e: The electric eel lives in rivers, streams and swamps, that is, in fresh water.
96685.m: The electric eel lives in fresh water.

96686.q: How does the electric eel breathe?
a: It gulps air at the surface of the water
Through its skin in the sand
96686.e: The electric eel has to come up regularly to gulp air. It breathes mainly through its mouth.
96686.m: The electric eel gulps air at the surface.

96687.q: Why should you never touch an electric eel?
a: It can give strong electric shocks
96687.e: A large electric eel can give very strong electric shocks. That can be dangerous for people too.
96687.m: An electric eel can give dangerous electric shocks.

96688.q: What does the electric eel use weak electric signals for?
a: To find its way in murky water
96688.e: With weak signals it senses its surroundings. That way it finds its way even in murky water.
96688.m: Weak electric signals help the electric eel find its way.

96689.q: What is a lightning conductor for?
a: To carry lightning safely into the ground
96689.e: The lightning conductor catches the lightning and carries the current safely into the earth through wires.
96689.m: A lightning conductor carries lightning into the ground.

96690.q: Where is a lightning conductor on a house?
a: In the garden under a stone
96690.e: The lightning conductor starts at the top of the roof, because lightning usually strikes high places.
96690.m: The lightning conductor starts on the roof.

96691.e: Benjamin Franklin is seen as the inventor of the lightning conductor. He developed it around 1750.
96691.m: Benjamin Franklin invented the lightning conductor.

96692.q: What does a lightning conductor mainly protect a house from?
a: A fire caused by a lightning strike
96692.e: If lightning strikes an unprotected house, the roof timbers, for example, can catch fire. The lightning conductor prevents this.
96692.m: A lightning conductor protects a house from fire caused by lightning.

96693.q: Which buildings very often have a lightning conductor?
96693.e: Tall buildings are hit by lightning especially often. That is why church towers are usually protected.
96693.m: Tall towers need a lightning conductor.

96694.q: What is the metal rod at the very top of a lightning conductor called?
96694.e: The air terminal sticks up above the roof and catches the lightning.
96694.m: The air terminal catches the lightning.

96695.q: What should you do with the wire of a lightning conductor in a thunderstorm?
a: Not touch it and keep your distance
Hold on to it with your hand
96695.e: When lightning strikes, a huge current flows through the wire. That is why you keep your distance in a thunderstorm.
96695.m: Don't touch the lightning conductor in a thunderstorm.

96696.q: What sprays from a burning sparkler on 1 August?
96696.e: In a sparkler, tiny metal particles burn and fly off as glowing sparks.

96697.q: What do you see with a small electric spark in the dark?
96697.e: A spark makes the air glow briefly. That is why you see a small light in the dark.

96698.q: Which part of a petrol engine makes sparks?
96698.e: The spark plug makes a spark that lights the mixture of petrol and air in the engine. The battery only supplies the electricity for it.
96698.m: The spark plug lights the petrol with a spark.

96699.q: Why should you be careful with sparks at a petrol station?
96699.e: Petrol fumes catch fire easily. Even a small spark can set them alight.
96699.m: Sparks and petrol are dangerous together.

96700.q: What do you often hear with a small electric spark?
a: A rushing sound like the sea
96700.e: The spark heats the air in a flash. That makes a small crack, like a tiny clap of thunder.
96700.m: A spark cracks like a tiny clap of thunder.

96701.q: What can you use to strike sparks for a fire?
a: Two pieces of wood in water
96701.e: If you strike steel against a flint, hot sparks fly. That is how people used to make fire.
96701.m: You strike sparks with flint and steel.

96702.q: Which appliance in the kitchen often lights gas with a spark?
96702.e: Many gas cookers have an igniter that makes a small spark. It lights the gas as it flows out.
96702.m: A gas cooker lights the gas with a spark.

96703.q: You shuffle across the carpet in socks and then touch the door handle. What sometimes jumps across with a crack?
96703.e: When you shuffle, your body gets charged. At the door handle, the charge jumps across as a small spark, which gives you a little nip.
96703.m: A spark can jump between your finger and the door handle.

96704.q: From where can you even see the northern and southern lights from above?
96704.e: Astronauts on the International Space Station see the polar lights glowing below them above the Earth.
96704.m: From space you see the polar lights from above.

96705.q: What are the polar lights in the north also called?
96705.e: The polar lights in the northern hemisphere are called the northern lights, those in the southern hemisphere the southern lights.
96705.m: In the north, the polar lights are called the northern lights.

96706.q: Can you sometimes see the northern lights in Switzerland too?
96706.e: During very strong solar storms, the northern lights reach as far as central Europe, for example in May 2024.
96706.m: In Switzerland, the northern lights are rarely seen.

96707.q: What do the northern lights often look like in the sky?
96707.e: The northern lights often form waving bands and arcs that look like curtains.
96707.m: The northern lights look like glowing curtains.

96708.q: What happens to a balloon that you rub on a woolly jumper?
96708.e: When you rub it, electrons move from the wool to the balloon. Afterwards it is charged.
96708.m: Rubbing a balloon on wool charges it.

96709.q: What happens to your hair when you hold a rubbed balloon above it?
96709.e: The charged balloon attracts the hair, so it rises up towards the balloon.

96710.q: Why does your hair stand up when you rub a balloon on it and then pull the balloon away?
a: The balloon blows air into the hair
The hair gets wet from rubbing
96710.e: When you rub, electrons move from the hair to the balloon. Afterwards the hair and the balloon have opposite charges and attract each other. This is called static electricity from friction.

96711.q: Which material charges a balloon especially well when you rub it?
96711.e: Wool easily gives off electrons when rubbed. That charges the balloon well.
96711.m: Wool is good for charging things up.

96712.q: What can a balloon rubbed on wool move without touching it?
96712.e: The charged balloon attracts a light can. The can then rolls along behind the balloon.
96712.m: A charged balloon can attract light things.

96713.q: What do you sometimes feel if you slide across a woollen sofa and then touch someone?
96713.e: Sliding charges you up. When you then touch someone, the charge evens out with a small shock.
96713.m: After rubbing, you can pass on a small shock.

96714.q: A balloon picks up electrons when it is rubbed on wool. How is it charged afterwards?
96714.e: Electrons are negatively charged. If the balloon gains extra electrons, it becomes negatively charged.
96714.m: A balloon with extra electrons is negatively charged.

96715.q: Roughly how long does a rubbed balloon stay stuck to the wall?
96715.e: The charge slowly flows away into the air and the wall. After a while the balloon falls down.
96715.m: A balloon's charge disappears over time.

96716.q: What happens if you hold a rubbed plastic comb over small scraps of paper?
96716.e: The comb became electrically charged while combing. It attracts the light scraps of paper.
96716.m: A charged comb attracts scraps of paper.

96717.q: What is the easiest way to charge a plastic comb?
96717.e: When you comb dry hair, the comb rubs against the hair. This makes it electrically charged.
96717.m: Combing dry hair charges the comb.

96718.q: What does a thin stream of water do if you hold a charged comb next to it?
96718.e: The charged comb attracts the water. That is why the thin stream bends towards the comb.
96718.m: A charged comb bends a stream of water.

96719.q: What material must the comb be made of for the paper scraps experiment?
96719.e: Plastic holds on to the charge. Metal would let the charge flow away through your hand.
96719.m: A plastic comb holds on to the charge.

96720.q: Why does the comb experiment work badly on damp days?
a: Damp air carries the charge away
96720.e: Moisture lets the charge flow away quickly. That is why the experiment works best in dry air.
96720.m: Damp air lets charge flow away.

96721.q: A comb is rubbed on dry hair. Afterwards it lifts small scraps of paper. Why?
a: The comb is electrically charged and attracts the paper
A draught blows the paper up
96721.e: Rubbing gives the comb an electric charge. The electric attraction is stronger than the small weight of the paper scraps.
96721.m: Electric attraction can lift light things.

96722.q: What happens to the paper scraps on the comb after a while?
96722.e: The scraps take on some charge from the comb. Then they repel each other and fall off.
96722.m: Scraps with the same charge fall off the comb again.

96723.q: Which things does a charged comb attract best?
96723.e: The electric force of the comb is weak. It is only enough for very light things such as paper or feathers.
96723.m: A charged comb only attracts light things.

a: A glow on pointed objects during a thunderstorm
96724.e: During a thunderstorm, pointed objects such as ships' masts can glow. This glow is called St Elmo's fire.
96724.m: St Elmo's fire is a glow on pointed objects during thunderstorms.

96725.q: Where did sailors in the past often see St Elmo's fire?
a: At the top of the ships' masts
96725.e: The tall masts of sailing ships were good places for the glow during thunderstorms.
96725.m: Sailors saw St Elmo's fire on the masts.

96726.q: What colour is St Elmo's fire usually?
96726.e: St Elmo's fire usually glows bluish or violet. It does not look like normal fire.

96727.q: Does anything really burn in St Elmo's fire?
a: No, it is an electrical glow
Yes, the air burns up completely
96727.e: St Elmo's fire is an electrical discharge in the air. Nothing burns.
96727.m: Nothing burns in St Elmo's fire.

96728.q: What does St Elmo's fire on a ship's mast show?
a: The air is strongly electrically charged
96728.e: St Elmo's fire glows when the air is strongly charged during a thunderstorm. Then there may also be lightning nearby.
96728.m: St Elmo's fire shows strongly charged air.

96729.q: Where can mountaineers see St Elmo's fire during a thunderstorm?
a: On the tip of their ice axe
In the snow under their feet
96729.e: Pointed objects such as an ice axe can glow or hum during a thunderstorm. This is a warning sign to look for shelter at once.
96729.m: A humming ice axe warns of lightning danger.

96730.q: In what weather does St Elmo's fire appear?
96730.e: St Elmo's fire appears when the air is strongly electrically charged during a thunderstorm.
96730.m: St Elmo's fire happens in thunderstorms.

96731.q: Where else can St Elmo's fire be seen today?
96731.e: Pilots sometimes see St Elmo's fire on the tips and edges of their aircraft when they fly through charged air.
96731.m: St Elmo's fire can also glow on aeroplanes.

96732.q: What did Benjamin Franklin fly during a thunderstorm?
96732.e: In 1752 Franklin flew a kite in a thunderstorm. He wanted to show that lightning is electrical.
96732.m: Franklin used a kite to show that lightning is electrical.

96733.q: Which country did Benjamin Franklin come from?
96733.e: Benjamin Franklin was born in Boston. He is one of the Founding Fathers of the United States.

96734.q: What did Franklin want to show with his kite experiment?
a: That lightning is made of electricity
That clouds are made of cotton wool
96734.e: Franklin thought that lightning was a huge electric spark. His experiment was meant to prove it.
96734.m: Franklin showed that lightning is electrical.

96735.q: Which kind of glasses is Benjamin Franklin said to have invented?
96735.e: Franklin is thought to have invented bifocals. With them you look through the top to see far away and through the bottom to see up close.
96735.m: Franklin's bifocals help you see near and far.

96736.q: In which century did Benjamin Franklin live?
96736.e: Franklin lived from 1706 to 1790, so in the 18th century.
96736.m: Benjamin Franklin lived in the 18th century.

96737.q: Why should you never copy Franklin's kite experiment?
96737.e: A kite in a thunderstorm can attract lightning. That is extremely dangerous.
96737.m: Flying a kite in a thunderstorm is extremely dangerous.

a: A rare kind of lightning that looks like a glowing ball
96738.e: Ball lightning is very rare. Scientists do not yet fully understand how it forms.
96738.m: Ball lightning is a rare glowing ball.

96739.q: What often picks up shortly before a thunderstorm?
96739.e: Just before the thunderstorm arrives, a strong, cool wind often suddenly starts to blow. Then it is time to find shelter.
96739.m: A strong wind often announces a thunderstorm.

96741.q: Which material hardly conducts electricity at all?
96741.e: Rubber barely lets electric charge through. That is why cables are covered in rubber or plastic.

96842.q: Into which two main groups are seismic waves divided?
96842.e: Body waves (P and S waves) travel through the Earth's interior. Surface waves spread along the Earth's surface and are slower.
96842.m: Seismic waves travel either through the Earth or along its surface.

96843.q: In which surface wave do the ground particles move in ellipses in the vertical plane?
96843.e: Rayleigh waves make the ground roll up and down like ocean waves. They were predicted by Lord Rayleigh in 1885.
96843.m: Rayleigh waves make the ground roll.

96844.q: Which surface wave moves the ground only horizontally and at right angles to the direction of travel?
96844.e: Love waves are horizontally polarised shear waves at the surface. The British mathematician Augustus Love described them in 1911.
96844.m: Love waves shake the ground sideways.

96845.q: Why do seismic waves travel along curved paths in the Earth's mantle?
a: They are attracted by the Moon.
96845.e: Because the rock deep down is more densely packed and stiffer, the waves travel faster. As a result they are constantly refracted and bend back towards the surface.
96845.m: Seismic rays curve because the waves get faster with depth.

96846.q: What is the method called that calculates three-dimensional images of the Earth's interior from many travel times of seismic waves?
96846.e: Similar to computed tomography in medicine, thousands of wave paths are analysed. Areas with faster or slower waves indicate cooler or hotter rock.
96846.m: Seismic tomography scans the Earth with earthquake waves.

96847.q: What is the graph called that shows the arrival time of seismic waves depending on the distance from the source?
96847.e: Travel time curves for P, S and other waves were created from many earthquakes worldwide. They are used to determine distances to the source and the structure of the Earth's interior.
96847.m: Travel time curves show when which wave arrives at which distance.

96848.q: Why do seismic waves become weaker the further they are from the source?
a: Their energy spreads out and is damped in the rock.
They are slowed down by the Earth's rotation.
They are absorbed by the magnetic field.
96848.e: The energy spreads over an ever larger wave front (geometric spreading). In addition, some of it is turned into heat by internal friction in the rock.
96848.m: Earthquake waves lose strength with distance.

96849.q: What is the minimum number of measuring stations needed to determine an epicentre with circles around the stations?
96849.e: From the difference in travel times, each station only gives a distance, that is, a circle. Only three circles intersect at a single clear point.
96849.m: With three stations an epicentre can be clearly located.

96850.q: What are the vibrations of the whole Earth called that can be measured for days after very strong earthquakes?
96850.e: They were first clearly measured after the 1960 Chile earthquake. The Earth then vibrates like a struck bell, with periods of up to about an hour.
96850.m: After very strong earthquakes the whole Earth rings like a bell.

96851.q: How do the particles vibrate in a P wave?
a: back and forth in the direction of travel
at right angles to the direction of travel
not at all, only the energy moves
96851.e: P waves are longitudinal waves: the rock is alternately compressed and stretched. They work in a similar way to sound waves.
96851.m: P waves are longitudinal waves like sound.

96852.q: What does the letter P stand for in P wave?
96852.e: The P wave is the fastest seismic wave and therefore arrives first at the seismometer. The name goes back to the Latin “undae primae”.
96852.m: The P wave is called the primary wave because it arrives first.

96853.q: In which substances can P waves travel?
96853.e: Every substance can be compressed, so pressure waves can travel everywhere. That is why P waves also pass through the liquid outer core.
96853.m: P waves pass through all states of matter.

96854.q: Who discovered the solid inner core of the Earth in 1936 from weak P waves in the shadow zone?
96854.e: The Danish seismologist noticed P waves that should not actually have arrived in the shadow zone. She explained them by reflections from an inner core.
96854.m: Inge Lehmann discovered the Earth's inner core.

96855.q: Where on Earth is the shadow zone in which hardly any direct P waves from an earthquake arrive?
a: In a ring on the side of the Earth facing away from the earthquake
96855.e: The liquid outer core deflects the P waves. This creates a ring far from the earthquake, roughly between 104 and 140 degrees away, where they hardly arrive directly.
96855.m: P waves have a ring-shaped shadow zone on the opposite side from the earthquake.

96856.q: Why does a shadow zone of P waves form?
a: They are strongly refracted at the liquid outer core.
They are swallowed by the magnetic field.
They are completely reflected by the Earth's crust.
They lose all their energy in the asthenosphere.
96856.e: When they enter the outer core their speed drops considerably, so they bend towards the centre. This creates an area that they do not reach directly.
96856.m: The core deflects P waves like a lens.

96857.q: How do earthquake early warning systems use the P wave?
a: It arrives before the destructive waves.
It announces an earthquake days in advance.
It stops the S wave from spreading.
96857.e: The location and strength of an earthquake are estimated from the first seconds of the P wave. Until the stronger S and surface waves arrive, there are a few seconds left for a warning.
96857.m: Early warning systems gain seconds because the P wave is faster.

96858.q: Roughly how fast does a P wave travel in water?
96858.e: In water the P wave is an ordinary sound wave at about 1500 m/s. In solid rock it is much faster.
96858.m: In water a P wave is simply sound.

96859.q: How do the particles vibrate in an S wave?
a: at right angles to the direction of travel
only vertically to the Earth's surface
96859.e: S waves are shear or transverse waves. The rock is shifted sideways, similar to a rope being shaken.

96860.q: Through which part of the Earth's interior can S waves not pass?
96860.e: S waves need a solid material that resists sideways deformation. This is not the case in the liquid outer core, so they end there.
96860.m: S waves do not pass through the liquid outer core.

96861.q: What can be determined from the time gap between the arrival of the P and S waves at a measuring station?
a: The distance to the earthquake source
The water temperature in the Earth's core
The length of the next earthquake
96861.e: P waves are faster than S waves, so the time gap grows with distance. The longer you wait between the two waves, the further away the source is.
96861.m: The bigger the gap between P and S waves, the further away the source.

96862.q: How do the rock particles in an S wave vibrate compared with the direction the wave is travelling?
a: At right angles to the direction of travel
Back and forth exactly in the direction of travel
Not at all, they stay still
Only in circles around the Earth's core
96862.e: S waves are shear or transverse waves: the particles move at right angles to the direction of travel. In P waves, by contrast, they vibrate in the direction of travel.
96862.m: S waves are transverse waves, P waves are longitudinal waves.

96863.q: Why do S waves often cause more damage to buildings than P waves?
a: They have larger amplitudes and shake sideways.
96863.e: Buildings are designed for vertical loads, and sideways shaking puts much more strain on them. In addition, the amplitudes of S waves are usually larger than those of P waves.
96863.m: Sideways shaking is especially dangerous for buildings.

96864.q: What does the letter S stand for in S wave?
96864.e: It is slower than the P wave and therefore arrives as the second wave. The word “shear” also fits.
96864.m: The S wave is called the secondary wave because it arrives second.

96865.q: What can be produced when a P wave hits a boundary between rock layers at an angle?
a: additional reflected and refracted S waves
an electric flash in the rock
a wave travelling at supersonic speed
96865.e: At boundaries, part of the energy is converted into the other type of wave (mode conversion). Additional arrivals then appear on seismograms.
96865.m: At layer boundaries, P waves can produce S waves.

96866.q: What do researchers conclude when S waves travel much more slowly in one area of the mantle than in the surrounding area?
a: The rock there is hotter and softer
There is a large cavity full of air there
The rock there is especially cold
There is a sea of water there
96866.e: Hot rock is less stiff, so shear waves become slower in it. This is how rising hot areas of the mantle beneath hotspots are found, for example.
96866.m: Slow S waves reveal hot rock in the mantle.

96867.q: Which event put Andrija Mohorovičić on the trail of the boundary between crust and mantle?
96867.e: While analysing the Pokupsko earthquake south of Zagreb on 8 October 1909, he noticed two groups of P waves. The faster one had travelled through a deeper layer with a higher speed.
96867.m: Mohorovičić discovered the base of the crust using earthquake waves.

96868.q: Roughly how deep is the Moho beneath the oceans?
96868.e: Oceanic crust is thin and consists mainly of basalt and gabbro. Beneath it, the mantle follows after just a few kilometres.
96868.m: Beneath the oceans the Earth's crust is only a few kilometres thick.

96869.q: On average, roughly how deep is the Moho beneath the continents?
96869.e: Continental crust is thicker and lighter than oceanic crust. On average it reaches about 35 km deep.
96869.m: Continental crust is several times thicker than oceanic crust.

96870.q: Roughly how deep does the Earth's crust reach beneath the Swiss Alps at its deepest points?
96870.e: Beneath mountain ranges the crust is thickened and forms a root. Seismic profiles show the Moho beneath the Alps at a depth of about 50 to 60 km.
96870.m: Beneath the Alps the crust reaches especially deep.

96871.q: How can the Moho be recognised using earthquake waves?
a: The waves suddenly become faster there
The waves turn into sound waves there
96871.e: In the dense mantle rock, P waves travel much faster than in the crust. This jump marks the boundary.
96871.m: At the Moho, P waves suddenly become faster.

96872.q: What mainly changes at the Moho?
a: the type of rock, from crustal rock to peridotite
the state of matter, from solid to liquid
the material, from rock to iron
the magnetisation, from north to south
96872.e: The Moho is mainly a boundary of chemical composition. Beneath it lies olivine-rich peridotite, which is denser than granite or basalt.
96872.m: The Moho separates crustal rock from mantle rock.

96873.q: What was the name of the US project in the 1960s that aimed to drill through the seabed down to the Moho?
96873.e: In 1961 the first test drilling in the deep ocean was carried out off Mexico. The project was stopped in 1966 because of the costs, and the Moho was never reached.
96873.m: Nobody has ever drilled down to the Moho.

96874.q: Where can rock from the Earth's mantle be studied at the surface without drilling?
96874.e: Ophiolites are pieces of oceanic lithosphere that were pushed onto continents during mountain building. Well-known examples are in Oman, but also in the Alps near Zermatt.
96874.m: Ophiolites show mantle rock at the surface.

96875.q: Which boundary in the Earth's interior separates the mantle from the outer core?
96875.e: In 1913 Beno Gutenberg determined the depth of the core-mantle boundary at about 2900 km. S waves disappear there because the outer core is liquid.
96875.m: The Gutenberg discontinuity separates the mantle and the core.

96876.q: Where does the name “asthenosphere” come from?
96876.e: The Greek word “asthenés” means feeble or weak. The layer is mechanically softer than the rigid plate above it.
96876.m: The asthenosphere is the weak layer of the mantle.

96877.q: At roughly what depth does the asthenosphere lie?
96877.e: It begins beneath the lithosphere, under the oceans from about 80 km, under the continents deeper. Its lower boundary is not sharp.
96877.m: The asthenosphere lies in the upper mantle.

96878.q: How does the asthenosphere show up in seismic measurements?
a: as a zone of reduced wave speed
as a zone without any waves at all
as a zone of greatly increased wave speed
as a zone with only surface waves
96878.e: In the so-called low-velocity zone, S waves in particular become slower. This points to softer, partly molten rock.
96878.m: In the asthenosphere, seismic waves become slower.

96879.q: Why can the asthenosphere be deformed even though it is mostly solid?
a: The rock is close to its melting point.
96879.e: The temperature is just below the melting temperature, and in places there is a little melt. Over a long time the rock can therefore flow slowly.
96879.m: The asthenosphere is hot enough to flow slowly.

96880.q: Why has Scandinavia been rising since the end of the last ice age?
a: The crust is springing back after the ice melted.
The Baltic Sea is slowly evaporating.
Volcanoes are pushing the land upwards.
The Earth's rotation is getting faster.
96880.e: The thick ice sheet had pressed the lithosphere down into the yielding asthenosphere. After the ice melted, mantle rock slowly flows back and the land rises (isostasy).
96880.m: After the ice age, Scandinavia is slowly rising again.

96881.q: Roughly how fast is the land on the Gulf of Bothnia rising today?
96881.e: In the area where the ice load used to be greatest, the uplift is up to almost 1 cm per year. As a result, the coastline there grows measurably out into the sea.
96881.m: Post-glacial uplift can easily be measured within a human lifetime.

96882.q: How do scientists work out how viscous the asthenosphere is?
a: From the slow uplift of regions after the ice age
From the colour of fresh lava
From the temperature of hot springs
From the height of ocean waves
96882.e: How fast Scandinavia or Canada rises after the ice has melted depends on the viscosity of the mantle. This gives a viscosity about 10 to the power of 23 times greater than that of water.
96882.m: Post-glacial uplift reveals how viscous the mantle is.

96883.q: Which layer of the Earth lies directly beneath the rigid lithosphere?
96883.e: The lithosphere includes the crust and the uppermost mantle and forms the plates. Beneath it comes the softer asthenosphere, on which the plates glide. The geologist Joseph Barrell introduced the term in 1914.
96883.m: The plates of the lithosphere glide on the asthenosphere.

96884.q: Roughly what is the maximum thickness of the oceanic lithosphere?
96884.e: At the mid-ocean ridges it is very thin. As it gets older it grows to a thickness of about 100 km.
96884.m: Old oceanic lithosphere is about 100 km thick.

96885.q: Why does oceanic lithosphere become thicker and heavier as it gets older?
96885.e: As it cools, upper mantle rock becomes rigid and is added to the lithosphere. At the same time the rock contracts, becomes denser and sinks deeper.
96885.m: Cooling makes oceanic plates thick, heavy and deep.

96886.q: Roughly how old is the oldest oceanic crust still present in the open ocean?
96886.e: The oldest parts lie in the western Pacific. Older oceanic lithosphere sank into subduction zones long ago.
96886.m: Ocean floors are much younger than continents.

96887.q: Which is the largest lithospheric plate by area?
96887.e: The Pacific Plate covers about 100 million square kilometres. It consists almost entirely of oceanic lithosphere.
96887.m: The Pacific Plate is the largest plate on Earth.

96888.q: Which smaller plate pushed against Europe from the south during the formation of the Alps?
96888.e: The Adriatic or Apulian Plate is often regarded as a spur of the African Plate. Its rock now forms parts of the Southern Alps, for example.
96888.m: The Adriatic Plate helped to shape the Alps.

96889.q: How does the lithosphere differ from the asthenosphere beneath it?
a: The lithosphere is cooler and rigid, the asthenosphere hotter and slowly deformable
The lithosphere is liquid, the asthenosphere solid
The lithosphere is made of iron, the asthenosphere of granite
96889.e: The boundary is mainly a temperature boundary at about 1300 °C. Below it the rock can creep slowly over long periods, and the plates glide on it.
96889.m: The rigid lithosphere glides on the slowly deformable asthenosphere.

96890.q: How thick can the lithosphere become beneath very old continental cores (cratons)?
96890.e: Beneath cratons such as those in Canada or South Africa, cool, rigid rock reaches especially deep. There the base of the lithosphere lies at 200 to 250 km.
96890.m: The lithosphere is thickest beneath old continents.

96891.q: How does the lithosphere react to a heavy load such as a large volcanic island?
a: It does not change at all.
96891.e: Like a loaded plank, the plate bends downwards beneath islands such as Hawaii. A trough forms around it, with a slight bulge further out.
96891.m: The lithosphere behaves like a flexible plate.

96892.q: How can the mostly solid mantle convect at all?
a: The rock creeps slowly over millions of years.
96892.e: At high temperatures, crystals deform very slowly through the movement of defects in their lattice. Over geological time the mantle therefore behaves like an extremely viscous liquid.
96892.m: The mantle flows even though it is solid.

96893.q: Which British geologist proposed mantle convection as the driving force of continental drift around 1930?
96893.e: Holmes realised that radioactive heat in the mantle can drive currents. With this he supplied a mechanism that Wegener's theory still lacked.
96893.m: Holmes explained continental drift with currents in the mantle.

96894.q: Why does hot mantle rock rise?
a: It expands and becomes less dense.
It is attracted by the magnetic field.
It is attracted by the Sun.
It contains gas bubbles like fizzy water.
96894.e: Heat makes the rock expand, and its density falls. Buoyancy makes it rise, while cooler, denser rock sinks.
96894.m: Hot rock rises, cold rock sinks.

96895.q: Which heat source mainly drives convection in the Earth's mantle?
a: Heat from radioactive decay and from the Earth's core
96895.e: Decaying elements such as uranium, thorium and potassium produce heat in the mantle. On top of that there is leftover heat from the formation of the Earth, which rises from the core.
96895.m: Radioactive heat and heat from the core drive mantle convection.

96896.q: What are the chimney-like upwellings of hot mantle rock thought to lie beneath Hawaii and Iceland called?
96896.e: Mantle plumes probably rise from great depth and partly melt beneath the plate. This creates volcanic areas away from the plate boundaries.
96896.m: Mantle plumes feed hotspots with hot rock.

96897.q: Which method do researchers use to create images of the inside of the Earth's mantle?
a: Deep boreholes down to the core
96897.e: Earthquake waves travel more slowly in hot rock and faster in cold rock. From many measuring stations worldwide, three-dimensional images of the mantle are calculated.
96897.m: Earthquake waves make the Earth's interior visible.

96898.q: What is the force called with which the raised mid-ocean ridges push the plates sideways?
96898.e: The ridges lie higher than the old ocean floor. The plates therefore glide downhill, as it were, which is why it is called “ridge push”.
96898.m: Mid-ocean ridges push the plates apart.

96899.q: What do tomographic images of sinking plates below a depth of 660 km show?
a: Some plates sink into the lower mantle.
All plates melt at a depth of 100 km.
The plates rise up again there.
There is no rock below 660 km.
96899.e: Beneath America and South-East Asia, cold remnants of plates can be seen almost down to the core-mantle boundary. This suggests that the whole mantle takes part in convection.
96899.m: Sinking plates can sink to the bottom of the mantle.

96900.q: At roughly what depth is the boundary between the Earth's mantle and core?
96900.e: The mantle reaches down to about 2900 km. Below it comes the liquid outer core of iron and nickel; the Earth's radius is about 6370 km.
96900.m: The Earth's mantle reaches down to about 2900 km.

96901.q: By how much is the axis of the magnetic dipole tilted against the Earth's axis of rotation today?
96901.e: The geomagnetic poles are currently about 9 to 10 degrees away from the geographic poles. The tilt changes slowly over time.
96901.m: The Earth's magnetic and geographic axes do not coincide.

96902.q: Roughly how strong is the Earth's magnetic field at the Earth's surface?
96902.e: The field is weakest at the equator and about twice as strong at the magnetic poles. A fridge magnet is a hundred to a thousand times stronger.
96902.m: The Earth's magnetic field is weak but measurable everywhere.

96903.q: Physically speaking, what kind of magnetic pole lies near the geographic North Pole?
96903.e: The north pole of a compass needle is attracted by the south pole of a magnet. The pole in the Arctic is called the Arctic magnetic pole, but physically it is a south pole.
96903.m: Physically, there is a magnetic south pole in the Arctic.

96904.q: In which direction has the Arctic magnetic pole moved in recent decades?
a: it stayed in the same place
96904.e: Since the 19th century it has been in northern Canada; around 2000 it reached speeds of over 50 km per year. In the meantime it has crossed the date line and is moving towards Siberia.
96904.m: The magnetic pole is constantly on the move.

96905.q: What is the area with a particularly weak magnetic field, where satellites are exposed to more radiation, called?
96905.e: Over the South Atlantic and South America, the inner radiation belt comes closer to the Earth. Satellites and the International Space Station experience more disturbances there.
96905.m: Over the South Atlantic the Earth's magnetic field is especially weak.

96906.q: What does the declination of a compass indicate?
a: the angle between magnetic north and geographic north
the angle at which the needle tilts towards the Earth's surface
the strength of the magnetic field
the error caused by iron in the casing
96906.e: The compass needle does not point exactly to geographic north. The declination varies with place and year and must be taken into account on maps.
96906.m: Declination is the difference between compass north and true north.

96907.q: What is the inclination of the Earth's magnetic field at a magnetic pole?
96907.e: The inclination is the angle between the field lines and the horizontal. At the magnetic poles the field lines run vertically, at the magnetic equator horizontally.
96907.m: At the magnetic pole a freely moving magnetic needle stands vertical.

96908.q: Why is the Earth's magnetic field also measured with satellites in space?
a: They record the field evenly all around the Earth
There is a stronger magnetic field in space
It cannot be measured on the ground at all
Satellites produce the magnetic field themselves
96908.e: There are measuring stations on the ground in only a few places and hardly any on the seas. Satellites such as ESA's three Swarm satellites circle the whole Earth.
96908.m: Satellites monitor the Earth's magnetic field worldwide.

96909.q: Which mathematician showed in 1839, using mathematical analysis, that the magnetic field mainly comes from the Earth's interior?
96909.e: Using spherical functions, Gauss split the field into parts coming from inside and outside. An old unit of magnetic flux density is also named after him.
96909.m: Gauss proved that the Earth's magnetic field comes from the Earth's interior.

96910.q: What does a dynamo in the Earth's core need to produce a magnetic field?
96910.e: Flowing liquid iron moves through a magnetic field and induces electric currents. These currents in turn produce the field and keep it going.
96910.m: The geodynamo turns the energy of flow into magnetic energy.

96911.q: Why can a permanent magnet inside the Earth not explain the Earth's magnetic field?
a: It is hotter there than the Curie temperature.
There are no metals in the core.
96911.e: Above the Curie temperature, about 770 °C for iron, substances lose their permanent magnetisation. In the core it is several thousand degrees.
96911.m: A hot Earth core cannot be a permanent magnet.

96912.q: Which force arranges the currents in the outer core into column-like vortices along the axis of rotation?
a: the frictional force of the crust
96912.e: Because the Earth rotates, the rising and sinking currents are deflected sideways. This arranges them in such a way that a large-scale dipole field forms.
96912.m: The Earth's rotation brings order to the currents in the core.

96913.q: Which energy source is mainly driving the geodynamo today?
a: the solidification of the inner core
96913.e: As the inner core grows, heat of crystallisation is released and lighter elements stay behind in the melt. Both make the liquid iron rise and convect.
96913.m: The growing inner core keeps the geodynamo going.

96914.q: What has happened during a reversal of the Earth's magnetic field?
a: The magnetic north and south poles have swapped places
The Earth has rotated the other way round
The magnetic field has disappeared for ever
96914.e: The magnetic field has reversed many times in the Earth's history. Computer models of the geodynamo show that such reversals can happen on their own.
96914.m: The Earth's magnetic field has reversed many times.

96915.q: How do we know that the Earth's outer core is liquid?
a: S waves from earthquakes cannot pass through it
People have drilled down to the core
96915.e: Shear waves (S waves) do not travel through liquids. That is why there is a shadow zone without S waves behind the core. The liquid outer core is over 2000 km thick.
96915.m: Earthquake waves reveal the liquid outer core.

96916.q: Why does Mars no longer have a global magnetic field today?
a: Its core dynamo has died out.
It is too close to the Sun.
